questions.question: A regular rhythm is recorded at 50 mm/s. Consecutive R waves are separated by 24 small horizontal squares. What is the ventricular rate?
options: 125/min
100/min
150/min
questions.explanation:
Paper Speed and Heart Rate

Correct answer: 125/min

Calculation

**At ==50 mm==/s, each ==1 mm== square is ==20 ms==.**

RR = 24 × 0.020 = 0.480 s; rate = 60/0.480 = **125/min**.

Technical Interpretation

**Check speed before intervals or rhythm rate.**

The familiar 1500/small-squares rule applies at ==25 mm==/s; at ==50 mm==/s use 3000/small squares.

**Gain controls voltage, not timing.**

Standard gain is ==10 mm==/mV; half or double gain changes apparent amplitude but not the RR interval.

**Use a timed strip for irregular rhythms**, rather than treating one RR interval as the average rate.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

questions.question: An asymptomatic patient has negative P, QRS and T waves in lead I, unexpectedly positive aVR and normal precordial R-wave progression. A previous ECG was normal. What should be suspected first?
options: Dextrocardia
Right-arm/left-arm electrode reversal
Left posterior fascicular block
Low atrial rhythm
questions.explanation:
Arm-Electrode Reversal

Correct answer: Right-arm/left-arm electrode reversal

Recognize the Technical Pattern

**RA/LA reversal inverts lead I**, exchanges II with III and aVR with aVL; aVF is unchanged.

Precordial leads retain their usual progression because chest electrodes have not been swapped.

Confirm Before Labeling Disease

**Check the electrode connections and repeat the ECG.**

Compare with prior tracings; do not diagnose a new axis disorder or infarction solely from the technically suspect tracing.

**Dextrocardia affects chest-lead progression** as well as limb orientation; deliberate right-sided recording requires documented placement.

Dextrocardia: Dextrocardia can invert lead I but usually also reverses normal precordial progression with standard left-sided chest placement; normal progression favors arm reversal.

Left posterior fascicular block: LPFB shifts the QRS axis but does not invert the entire P–QRS–T sequence in lead I or exchange aVR/aVL relationships.

Low atrial rhythm: A low atrial focus changes P-wave polarity and may shorten PR; it does not explain simultaneous reversal of ventricular depolarization and repolarization in lead I.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

questions.question: A monitor displays rapid wide oscillations, but the patient is alert with a regular palpable pulse at 78/min. Narrow QRS complexes continue at that rate through the oscillations in another lead. What is the best immediate interpretation?
options: Hemodynamically tolerated sustained VT
Movement artifact superimposed on the underlying rhythm
Atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction
Pre-excited atrial fibrillation
questions.explanation:
Tremor Artifact Mimicking Tachycardia

Correct answer: Movement artifact superimposed on the underlying rhythm

Reconcile Electrical and Clinical Data

**Assess the patient and pulse immediately.**

A monitor appearance alone is insufficient; inspect multiple leads for unaffected complexes marching through noise.

Restore Signal Quality

**Correct tremor, cable motion and poor electrode contact**, then obtain a diagnostic tracing.

**Do not let apparent stability alone exclude real VT.**

The decisive evidence here is the preserved underlying electrical/pulse rhythm, not merely a conscious patient.

**If perfusion is absent or unstable**, act on the emergency assessment while checking signal validity; artifact recognition must not delay needed resuscitation.

Hemodynamically tolerated sustained VT: Stable VT is possible, but persistent normal QRS complexes and a pulse matching the slower underlying rhythm strongly favor artifact here.

Atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction: True rapid ventricular conduction would alter the ventricular/pulse rate; the preserved slower QRS sequence contradicts a 1:1 tachycardia.

Pre-excited atrial fibrillation: Pre-excited AF produces an irregular rapid ventricular rhythm with variable QRS morphology, not an independent unchanged regular QRS sequence beneath noise.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

questions.question: QRS is predominantly positive in lead I, negative in aVF and positive in lead II. Which axis range best fits?
options: Between −30° and 0°
Between −90° and −30°
Between +90° and +180°
Between −180° and −90°
questions.explanation:
Refining the Frontal QRS Axis

Correct answer: Between −30° and 0°

Stepwise Axis Assessment

**I positive/aVF negative** places the axis in the left-superior quadrant.

Lead II positivity narrows it to −30° to 0°, usually still within the normal adult range.

Clinical Limits

**Axis is a vector description, not a diagnosis.**

LAFB, infarction, hypertrophy, pre-excitation and lead errors can alter it.

**Check calibration and limb placement**, then integrate QRS morphology and clinical context.

An isoelectric lead can refine the estimate: the mean axis lies approximately perpendicular to that lead, with polarity resolving the direction.

I | aVF | Initial quadrant

+ | + | 0° to +90°

+ | − | −90° to 0°; inspect II

− | + | +90° to +180°

− | − | Extreme superior axis

Between −90° and −30°: More negative left-axis deviation would make lead II negative; its positive QRS refines this case to above −30 degrees.

Between +90° and +180°: Right-axis deviation produces a negative lead I with positive aVF, the opposite of the supplied limb-lead pattern.

Between −180° and −90°: Extreme superior axis has negative QRS in both I and aVF; lead I is positive here.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

questions.question: A tracing shows QRS 104 ms, axis −60°, qR complexes in I/aVL and rS complexes in II/III/aVF. Which conduction abnormality best fits?
options: Left anterior fascicular block
Complete left bundle-branch block
Left posterior fascicular block
Complete right bundle-branch block
questions.explanation:
Left Anterior Fascicular Block

Correct answer: Left anterior fascicular block

Activation Sequence

**Delayed anterior-superior LV activation** produces a left-superior mean axis.

Typical axis is −45° to −90°, qR in I/aVL and rS inferiorly; QRS is usually ==<120 ms==.

Interpretation and Follow-up

**Consider ischemic, hypertensive, degenerative or structural disease.**

An isolated fascicular pattern does not prove the underlying cause.

**RBBB plus LAFB is bifascicular disease.**

Syncope, alternating bundle patterns or advanced AV block require evaluation beyond an incidental isolated LAFB finding.

**Exclude lead errors and infarct-related axis shifts** when morphology or clinical history is discordant.

Complete left bundle-branch block: Complete LBBB requires a wider QRS with characteristic broad lateral R waves and loss of normal lateral septal q waves; the supplied narrow qR pattern favors LAFB.

Left posterior fascicular block: LPFB causes rightward rather than left-superior axis, with rS in I/aVL and qR inferiorly after excluding other right-axis causes.

Complete right bundle-branch block: RBBB needs delayed terminal rightward activation, typically rSR-prime in V1 and broad terminal S in I/V6 with QRS ≥120 ms; these are not supplied.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: An asymptomatic adult has RBBB, LAFB and PR 240 ms. What can be concluded from the surface ECG alone?
options: Complete AV block with a junctional escape
Definite failure of all three fascicles
Bifascicular block with first-degree AV delay; the PR delay is not necessarily in the remaining fascicle
Isolated AV nodal disease explaining every finding
questions.explanation:
Bifascicular Block With Long PR

Correct answer: Bifascicular block with first-degree AV delay; the PR delay is not necessarily in the remaining fascicle

Avoid Overlocalization

**PR includes atrial, AV nodal and His–Purkinje conduction.**

A long PR does not locate the delay; the label “trifascicular block” can overstate what the surface ECG proves.

Assess Risk Clinically

**Review symptoms, prior ECGs and reversible causes.**

Syncope or intermittent advanced block changes the evaluation; routine pacing is not established solely by this asymptomatic combination.

**EPS can measure HV conduction in selected patients.**

Alternating bundle-branch block provides stronger evidence of extensive distal disease than PR prolongation alone.

Complete AV block with a junctional escape: Complete AV block requires absence of conducted atrial impulses and independent rhythms; this patient has first-degree delay with maintained conduction.

Definite failure of all three fascicles: PR prolongation can arise in the AV node; the ECG does not prove that the remaining left posterior fascicle is diseased.

Isolated AV nodal disease explaining every finding: AV nodal delay may explain PR prolongation but cannot itself account for the documented right bundle and left anterior fascicular patterns.

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: QT is 400 ms and RR is 512 ms. What is the Fridericia-corrected QT?
options: 400 ms
500 ms
559 ms
781 ms
questions.explanation:
Fridericia QT Correction

Correct answer: 500 ms

Calculation

**QTcF = QT / cube root(RR), with intervals in seconds.**

QT = 0.400 s; RR = 0.512 s; cube root(0.512) = 0.800. QTcF = 0.400/0.800 = **0.500 s = ==500 ms==**.

Interpretation

**Bazett uses square root(RR)** and often overcorrects in tachycardia.

Here QTcB is approximately ==559 ms==; the formula difference is clinically relevant.

**QTc around ==500 ms== warrants review** of drugs, electrolytes, symptoms and clinical risk.

It does not alone prove congenital long QT syndrome; verify T-wave end and exclude a separate U wave.

AHA ECG Monitoring Practice Standards, 2017 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000527

questions.question: A patient with chronic LBBB has QRS 168 ms and an automated QTc of 525 ms. Which approach best evaluates whether repolarization itself is excessively prolonged?
options: Diagnose congenital long QT syndrome from the automated QTc alone
Manual assessment using a QRS-adjusted QT or JT-based approach
Treat the uncorrected QT as independent of heart rate
Exclude all arrhythmic risk because LBBB explains any QT prolongation
questions.explanation:
QT Assessment With a Wide QRS

Correct answer: Manual assessment using a QRS-adjusted QT or JT-based approach

Separate Depolarization and Repolarization

**QT = QRS duration + JT interval.**

A wide QRS lengthens QT through activation delay, so unadjusted QTc can exaggerate repolarization abnormality.

Practical Assessment

**Measure manually and apply a validated adjustment**, with rate correction appropriate to the method.

Different formulas have limitations; use a consistent approach and seek electrophysiology input for difficult cases.

**Review the clinical substrate**, drugs, electrolytes and prior tracings.

No single adjusted cutoff substitutes for symptoms, documented arrhythmias or a family history of sudden death.

Diagnose congenital long QT syndrome from the automated QTc alone: The QT includes delayed depolarization; wide QRS can inflate QT without equivalent repolarization prolongation, so syndrome diagnosis needs more evidence.

Treat the uncorrected QT as independent of heart rate: QT remains rate-dependent despite bundle-branch block; omitting rate assessment introduces a separate measurement error.

Exclude all arrhythmic risk because LBBB explains any QT prolongation: LBBB confounds measurement but does not prevent concurrent drug/electrolyte-related repolarization delay or ventricular arrhythmia risk.

AHA ECG Monitoring Practice Standards, 2017 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000527

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: A P wave is 136 ms wide with notching in lead II and a terminal negative component in V1 that is 1.2 mm deep and 48 ms wide. Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: Definite mitral stenosis
Left atrial electrical abnormality; imaging is needed to establish anatomical enlargement
Isolated right atrial enlargement
Normal P waves because duration remains below 200 ms
questions.explanation:
Left Atrial Abnormality Versus Interatrial Delay

Correct answer: Left atrial electrical abnormality; imaging is needed to establish anatomical enlargement

Electrical Criteria

**Broad/notched P in II and excessive terminal negative P force in V1** support left atrial abnormality.

A terminal negative component ==≥1 mm== deep and ==≥40 ms== wide is a useful conventional criterion.

Anatomy Is Not Guaranteed

**Conduction delay can broaden P without major chamber enlargement.**

Advanced interatrial block typically has P ==≥120 ms== with positive–negative inferior P waves.

**Echo quantifies atrial size and valve disease.**

Hypertension, mitral disease, diastolic dysfunction and cardiomyopathy can contribute; the historical term P mitrale is not specific for mitral stenosis.

Definite mitral stenosis: This P-wave pattern can accompany many left-atrial loading conditions and interatrial delay; it does not identify a specific valve lesion.

Isolated right atrial enlargement: RA abnormality primarily increases early/positive P forces, often with inferior height >2.5 mm; the prolonged terminal negative component favors left-atrial involvement.

Normal P waves because duration remains below 200 ms: The 200 ms threshold applies to PR, not P duration; a P wave ≥120 ms is prolonged.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

questions.question: An asymptomatic endurance athlete has S(V1)+R(V5) of 38 mm, normal repolarization and no pathological Q waves or family history. What is the best interpretation of the voltage finding alone?
options: It meets a conventional LVH voltage criterion but does not prove pathological hypertrophy
It establishes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
It is uninterpretable because athletes cannot meet ECG LVH criteria
It establishes hypertensive LVH despite normal blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Voltage Criteria and Athletic Remodeling

Correct answer: It meets a conventional LVH voltage criterion but does not prove pathological hypertrophy

Voltage Thresholds

**Sokolow–Lyon:** S(V1)+larger R(V5/V6) ==≥35 mm==.

Cornell voltage: R(aVL)+S(V3) ==>28 mm== in men or ==>20 mm== in women; recording gain must be standard.

Recognize Limits

**Sensitivity and specificity depend on body habitus and training.**

Obesity/COPD can mask voltage; young thin athletes can have high voltage without disease.

**Repolarization abnormalities, symptoms or family history change the concern.**

Lateral strain, marked T inversion or other abnormal findings warrant directed assessment; echocardiography/CMR establishes anatomy when indicated.

It establishes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Isolated high voltage is common in trained or thin individuals; HCM requires structural/clinical evidence rather than a voltage sum alone.

It is uninterpretable because athletes cannot meet ECG LVH criteria: The voltage can be measured and reported; the limitation is specificity for disease, not whether the criterion can be calculated.

It establishes hypertensive LVH despite normal blood pressure: Hypertension is one cause of LVH, but ECG voltage cannot infer an unrecorded pressure history or establish anatomical mass by itself.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

questions.question: A patient with chronic pulmonary hypertension has right axis deviation, R/S >1 in V1, deep S waves in V5–V6 and right-precordial T inversion. There is no acute chest pain or dynamic ST change. Which explanation best fits?
options: Isolated posterior myocardial infarction
Right ventricular hypertrophy with strain
Isolated left anterior fascicular block
Typical complete LBBB
questions.explanation:
Tall R Wave in V1

Correct answer: Right ventricular hypertrophy with strain

Integrate the Pattern

**RVH:** right axis, dominant R in V1 and persistent lateral S waves.

RA abnormality and anterior ST–T strain strengthen the interpretation in pulmonary hypertension.

Tall R Differential

**Posterior infarction, RBBB, pre-excitation and lead errors** can also produce a tall R in V1.

**One voltage finding is insufficient.**

Check QRS width, delta wave, terminal R-prime, chest-lead placement and symptoms.

**Echo confirms RV structure and function**; ECG cannot quantify pulmonary pressure or exclude PE by itself.

Isolated posterior myocardial infarction: Posterior infarction can produce tall anterior R waves but typically needs compatible ischemic context and reciprocal ST changes; the rightward forces and strain pattern support RVH here.

Isolated left anterior fascicular block: LAFB shifts the axis superior-leftward; it does not account for right axis, dominant anterior RV forces and lateral S waves.

Typical complete LBBB: LBBB usually produces a predominantly negative V1 complex with broad lateral R waves; that activation pattern is opposite to the supplied dominant rightward forces.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

questions.question: According to the Fifth Universal Definition of MI (2026), which statement describes the classical pathological Q-wave criterion?
options: Duration ≥20 ms in any limb lead regardless of depth
Depth ≥2 mm alone in any single lead
Duration ≥40 ms and/or depth ≥25% of the R wave, assessed in contiguous leads
Any Q wave in a lateral lead
questions.explanation:
Pathological Q Waves in the 2026 Universal Definition

Correct answer: Duration ≥40 ms and/or depth ≥25% of the R wave, assessed in contiguous leads

Current Definition

**2026 classical criterion:** Q duration ==≥40 ms== and/or depth ==≥25%== of the same-lead R wave.

Assess two contiguous leads and the full clinical/imaging context; isolated findings require caution.

Do Not Equate Every Q Wave With Infarction

**HCM, pre-excitation, conduction abnormalities and lead misplacement** can produce noninfarct Q waves.

**A prior MI diagnosis needs compatible evidence.**

CMR/echo scar or regional dysfunction can clarify; absence of Q waves does not exclude a previous infarct.

**Late acute-occlusion presentations may show Q waves/T inversion** rather than persistent ST elevation; ongoing symptoms still require urgent assessment.

Duration ≥20 ms in any limb lead regardless of depth: This lower duration threshold without distribution/context is not the classical definition adopted in the cited 2026 document.

Depth ≥2 mm alone in any single lead: An isolated absolute depth threshold does not represent the stated classical criterion and can misclassify normal or noninfarct Q waves.

Any Q wave in a lateral lead: Small lateral septal q waves can be physiological; their presence alone does not establish infarction.

Fifth Universal Definition of MI, 2026 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.07.025

questions.question: A patient with complete AV block has intermittent very large right atrial pressure waves aligned with P waves that occur during ventricular systole. Which mechanism explains these waves?
options: Rapid passive right atrial emptying after tricuspid opening
Systolic regurgitant flow through an incompetent tricuspid valve
Atrial contraction into a persistently stiff but accessible right ventricle
Atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve
questions.explanation:
Cannon a Waves and Atrioventricular Timing

Correct answer: Atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve

Identify the Event Before Naming the Wave

**The a wave represents atrial contraction.** When contraction occurs against a closed tricuspid valve, a large cannon wave can result.

Complete AV block permits changing atrial–ventricular timing, so giant waves may be intermittent. Other rhythms can also produce unfavorable timing; the wave alone does not establish complete heart block.

Distinguish these waves from consistently prominent a waves caused by resistance to atrial emptying and from systolic regurgitant v waves.

Correlate the Pressure Trace With the ECG

**Use simultaneous rhythm and waveform timing**, rather than identifying every tall wave by amplitude alone.

The x descent relates to atrial relaxation and systolic annular motion; the y descent reflects atrial emptying after the tricuspid valve opens.

Assess the patient’s rate, perfusion and rhythm independently of the waveform label. A conduction disorder may require urgent treatment, but a cannon wave is a mechanistic clue rather than a complete management prescription. Catheter motion and artifact should be excluded when a pressure deflection lacks a plausible relationship to the ECG. Document timing and reproducibility so that subsequent clinicians can distinguish a genuine hemodynamic sign from a nonspecific description of prominent venous pulsation.

Wave or descent | Principal event | Useful distinction

a wave | Atrial contraction | Prominent with resistance to atrial emptying

Cannon a wave | Atrial contraction against closed tricuspid valve | Correlate with AV timing

v wave | Atrial filling during ventricular systole | Large with TR on right side; left-sided size also depends on compliance

x descent | Atrial relaxation and systolic annular displacement | Interpret in rhythm and disease context

y descent | Emptying after AV valve opening | Rapid early ventricular filling

Rapid passive right atrial emptying after tricuspid opening: Passive emptying generates the y descent, a fall in pressure after valve opening rather than a large P-linked pressure rise during ventricular systole.

Systolic regurgitant flow through an incompetent tricuspid valve: Tricuspid regurgitation produces prominent systolic v or fused c-v waves; the intermittent P-linked waves during AV dissociation instead identify cannon a waves.

Atrial contraction into a persistently stiff but accessible right ventricle: Poor RV compliance can produce prominent a waves on each appropriately timed atrial contraction, whereas the intermittent giant waves here track unfavorable AV timing.

Merck Manual professional: cardiovascular examination — https://www.merckmanuals.com/en-ca/professional/cardiovascular-disorders/approach-to-the-cardiac-patient/cardiovascular-examination

questions.topic: Sinus node dysfunction and physiological bradycardia
questions.question: A high-quality rhythm strip shows identical sinus P waves with a stable P–P interval of 800 ms. Repeated pauses between visible P waves measure 1600 ms, with no intervening premature atrial activity. Conducted beats have unchanged PR intervals. Which mechanism is most consistent with this pattern?
options: Sinus arrest
Second-degree type II sinoatrial exit block
Second-degree Mobitz II AV block
A blocked premature atrial complex
questions.explanation:
Second-Degree Sinoatrial Exit Block

Correct answer: Second-degree type II sinoatrial exit block

Use Atrial Timing Rather Than the Ventricular Pause Alone

**Sinoatrial exit block is failure of a sinus impulse to activate adjacent atrial tissue.** Sinus node activity is not directly visible on the surface ECG; the mechanism is inferred from the atrial timing pattern.

With a stable baseline cycle, a type II pattern produces a missing P–QRS–T sequence and a pause that is an integral multiple of the preceding P–P interval. Here 1600 ms equals two cycles of 800 ms.

Sinus arrest concerns impulse formation rather than exit conduction. Coincidental timing, sinus arrhythmia and concealed atrial ectopy limit certainty, so a compatible pattern is more defensible than claiming direct proof of sinus-node depolarization.

Distinguish Related Conduction Patterns

**Inspect P waves, including the preceding T waves, before labeling a pause.** A blocked atrial premature beat can mimic sinus node disease, while AV block retains atrial depolarizations during ventricular pauses.

Sinoatrial Wenckebach typically shows grouped atrial beating with shortening P–P intervals before the pause. First-degree sinoatrial delay cannot be diagnosed reliably from an ordinary surface strip.

Clinical management depends on attributable symptoms, reversible causes and the broader rhythm evaluation, not the exit-block label alone. Review rate-slowing drugs, autonomic triggers and systemic disease. Symptomatic recurrent pauses require monitored assessment and consideration of pacing after the mechanism and indication are established. A technically uncertain strip should prompt better recording rather than an irreversible treatment decision from one apparent gap.

Pause pattern | Useful distinction

Type II SA exit block | Stable P–P cycle; missing atrial cycle; pause an integral multiple

Sinus arrest | Pause not required to preserve baseline cycle

AV block | P waves continue during absent ventricular responses

Blocked atrial ectopy | Premature abnormal P may distort the preceding T wave

Sinus arrest: Failure of sinus impulse formation produces a pause whose duration need not preserve the previous sinus cycle. A reproducible exact multiple of a stable atrial cycle instead supports exit block, although surface ECG inference is not absolute.

Second-degree Mobitz II AV block: Mobitz II AV block causes nonconducted P waves while atrial activity continues. The pause here involves missing atrial depolarization rather than visible P waves failing to conduct to the ventricles.

A blocked premature atrial complex: A premature atrial depolarization can be hidden in the preceding T wave and produce an apparent pause. Careful recording here excludes intervening premature activity and shows repeated preservation of the underlying sinus-cycle timing.

ACC/AHA/HRS electrophysiology data definitions, 2006 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2006.09.020

ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia and conduction-delay guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628

questions.question: A rhythm strip appears to show ventricular pauses after every sinus beat. Magnification reveals a small abnormal atrial deflection deforming each preceding T wave, earlier than the next expected sinus P wave. These early deflections have no following QRS. Which diagnosis best explains the pattern?
options: Sinus arrest with junctional escape
Two-to-one AV block of sinus impulses
Second-degree sinoatrial exit block
Blocked atrial bigeminy
questions.explanation:
Blocked Atrial Premature Beats Mimicking AV Block

Correct answer: Blocked atrial bigeminy

Find the Premature P Wave

**An atrial premature impulse can reach refractory AV tissue and fail to conduct.** Its P wave may be hidden in the ST segment or T wave, creating apparent sinus slowing or a ventricular pause.

Compare the suspicious T wave with unaffected beats in several leads. Assess atrial timing, morphology and coupling rather than relying on the ventricular rate or an automated AV-block label.

Sinus-node resetting by the premature impulse can alter the following interval. A pause after an early atrial beat should not be assumed to be a fixed-multiple SA block or intrinsic His–Purkinje failure.

Avoid Treating a Mimic as Advanced Conduction Disease

**Confirm the mechanism before selecting permanent pacing.** A blocked premature atrial beat does not carry the same implication as nonreversible Mobitz II or high-grade block.

Assess symptoms, ectopic burden, medication triggers and structural findings as appropriate. Stable incidental ectopy and symptomatic frequent blocked bigeminy require different levels of intervention.

Specialist rhythm treatment, including selected ablation, may be considered when frequent ectopy produces clinically important symptoms or dysfunction; isolated case reports do not define a universal treatment regimen. Preserve a high-quality tracing and reconsider the diagnosis if the presumed block changes with careful atrial inspection. Concurrent true conduction disease remains possible, so finding ectopy does not excuse ignoring separate documented high-grade block or unexplained syncope.

Sinus arrest with junctional escape: Sinus arrest concerns failure of sinus impulse formation and may be followed by escape activity. It does not explain the repeated early abnormal atrial deflections that account for the apparent blocked-beat pattern here.

Two-to-one AV block of sinus impulses: In true 2:1 AV block, sinus P waves occur at the underlying atrial cycle and every other impulse fails to conduct. Here the nonconducted atrial deflection is premature and morphologically different, identifying ectopy rather than alternate block of regular sinus impulses.

Second-degree sinoatrial exit block: SA exit block produces absent expected atrial activation, with a compatible relationship to the sinus cycle. The visible premature atrial activity hidden in the T wave supplies another mechanism for the apparent pause.

ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia and conduction-delay guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628

bullets.text: **An atrial premature impulse can reach refractory AV tissue and fail to conduct.** Its P wave may be hidden in the ST segment or T wave, creating apparent sinus slowing or a ventricular pause.

questions.question: A patient with sinus rhythm has PR 360 ms and one-to-one AV conduction. During exercise, the PR remains markedly prolonged and fatigue is reproduced despite an adequate sinus-rate rise. LV systolic function is preserved and there is no inducible ischemia. Which mechanism most plausibly links the conduction finding to symptoms?
options: Ventricular dyssynchrony from bundle-branch block
Chronotropic incompetence
Intermittent complete AV block
Poor atrioventricular timing impairing filling and forward output
questions.explanation:
Marked First-Degree AV Delay and AV Dyssynchrony

Correct answer: Poor atrioventricular timing impairing filling and forward output

Delay Can Matter Despite One-to-One Conduction

**First-degree AV block is more accurately AV delay because every atrial impulse still conducts.** Its conventional definition is ==PR >200 ms==.

Marked prolongation, often around ==300 ms or more==, can produce unfavorable atrial–ventricular timing, reduced effective filling and increased filling pressures. This resembles pacemaker syndrome despite the absence of an implanted device.

The numerical boundary is not an automatic implantation trigger. Demonstrating a plausible symptom relationship, particularly during activity when delay persists, is central to clinical significance.

Evaluate Before Selecting Pacing

**Review drugs, conduction pattern, structural disease and alternative sources of fatigue.** Exercise assessment can link symptoms with persistent long AV timing and distinguish a deficient sinus response.

A narrow QRS often suggests nodal delay, but PR duration alone does not definitively localize the abnormality. A new wide QRS, syncope or higher-grade block changes risk assessment.

Selected patients with symptoms attributable to marked delay may benefit from pacing assessment after reversible contributors are addressed; supporting evidence is more limited than for nonreversible high-grade block. Asymptomatic first-degree delay or symptoms unrelated to it should not be treated with a pacemaker solely to normalize the ECG. If pacing is chosen, consider how restoring AV timing interacts with ventricular pacing burden and ventricular function, rather than correcting one interval at the expense of unnecessary dyssynchrony.

Ventricular dyssynchrony from bundle-branch block: Intraventricular activation delay can impair ventricular efficiency, particularly with a wide LBBB pattern. The supplied abnormality is a markedly long PR; a bundle-branch mechanism should not be inferred without its ECG evidence.

Chronotropic incompetence: An inadequate sinus-rate response can produce exertional symptoms, but the monitored exercise response is adequate here. The prominent abnormality is atrioventricular timing rather than failure to increase sinus rate.

Intermittent complete AV block: Complete block requires failure of atrial impulses to conduct with independent ventricular activation. The recorded symptomatic exercise period retains one-to-one conduction, so that mechanism is not demonstrated.

questions.question: A strip has a stable sinus P–P interval. Successive conducted PR intervals measure 180, 220 and 260 ms, followed by a nonconducted P wave. The next conducted PR is 180 ms. Which interpretation best fits?
options: Second-degree sinoatrial Wenckebach block
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz II
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I
Blocked atrial bigeminy
questions.explanation:
Wenckebach and Mobitz II: Conducted PR Intervals

Correct answer: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I

Read Atrial Timing and AV Conduction Together

**Mobitz I describes progressive AV conduction delay culminating in a blocked atrial impulse, followed by shorter conduction time when the sequence restarts.** The supplied PR progression and reset form a classic Wenckebach sequence.

Mobitz II requires stable conducted PR intervals around an intermittently blocked sinus impulse, with attention to a stable atrial rate and exclusion of mimics. A pure 2:1 strip cannot establish either type from PR progression alone.

Review enough cycles to avoid mistaking subtle PR changes, concealed ectopy or vagal slowing for a different mechanism. An automated label is not a substitute for examining atrial activity.

Separate ECG Pattern From Anatomical Risk

**Mobitz I is commonly nodal, especially with a narrow QRS, but can occasionally be infranodal.** Mobitz II generally signals His–Purkinje disease and has a different progression risk.

Assess symptoms, QRS pattern, reversible causes and response to exercise or selected electrophysiological testing when localization is consequential. A wide QRS alone does not convert a Wenckebach sequence into Mobitz II.

Asymptomatic nodal Wenckebach often warrants observation and cause review, whereas nonreversible Mobitz II, advanced block or complete block can require pacing regardless of symptoms. Hemodynamic compromise demands immediate stabilization before a detailed outpatient localization strategy. Preserve both descriptions in the clinical record: what the strip shows and what the total evidence suggests about the site and risk of block.

Pattern | Atrial activity and conducted PR

Mobitz I | Progressive PR delay, blocked P, then shorter PR

Mobitz II | Stable sinus timing; conducted PR constant around blocked impulse

2:1 AV block | Alternate P waves blocked; no sufficient consecutive PR sequence to type

Blocked PAC | Premature abnormal P rather than a regular sinus impulse

Second-degree sinoatrial Wenckebach block: SA Wenckebach concerns atrial timing and missing atrial activation. Here P waves continue at a stable cycle and the changing PR interval demonstrates progressive delay between atrial and ventricular activation.

Second-degree AV block, Mobitz II: Mobitz II has a nonconducted sinus impulse without the demonstrated progressive PR prolongation; conducted PR intervals before and after the blocked beat remain constant in a correctly classified pattern.

Blocked atrial bigeminy: Blocked premature atrial beats are early and usually have a different atrial morphology or deform the preceding T wave. The nonconducted P here occurs on the stable sinus schedule after progressive AV delay.

questions.question: A continuous ECG strip shows regular sinus P waves at 80/min with alternate P waves nonconducted. Conducted PR intervals are 190 ms and QRS duration is 132 ms. No sequence with two consecutive conducted P waves is available. Which description is most defensible?
options: Two-to-one AV block with the anatomical level not established by this strip
Mobitz II AV block established by the constant conducted PR intervals
Mobitz I AV block established by the ventricular rate of forty
Infranodal block established by the wide QRS
questions.explanation:
Two-to-One AV Block: Limits of Surface Classification

Correct answer: Two-to-one AV block with the anatomical level not established by this strip

Describe What the Recording Actually Demonstrates

**Two-to-one conduction is a pattern, not proof of either Mobitz subtype.** Alternate atrial impulses are blocked, preventing observation of the consecutive PR behavior needed for the usual type I/type II distinction.

Verify regular sinus activity and exclude premature blocked atrial beats, artifact and concealed ectopy. Measure QRS and conducted PR, but do not use either alone as an anatomical verdict.

Review longer telemetry for another conduction ratio or a diagnostic sequence. A transition can provide information unavailable from the short pure 2:1 segment.

Localize When It Changes Risk and Treatment

**The site of block matters because infranodal disease can progress with an unreliable escape rhythm.** Symptoms, structural disease and associated conduction abnormalities determine urgency.

Selected stable patients can undergo supervised exercise testing; improved conduction supports a nodal site, while deterioration raises concern for infranodal disease. EPS can resolve consequential uncertainty when surface assessment remains insufficient.

Do not use diagnostic uncertainty as a reason to delay stabilization of a compromised patient. Conversely, do not implant solely from an unsupported Mobitz II label when the stable clinical setting calls for clarification. Nonreversible infranodal 2:1 block and asymptomatic convincingly nodal 2:1 block have different management implications. Document the measured pattern and the evidence for localization separately so later decisions do not inherit an unproven interpretation.

Mobitz II AV block established by the constant conducted PR intervals: In a pure 2:1 pattern, each conducted PR is separated by a blocked impulse; there is no consecutive conducted sequence to assess Wenckebach progression. Constant visible PR values alone therefore do not establish Mobitz II.

Mobitz I AV block established by the ventricular rate of forty: A ventricular rate of forty follows from alternate conduction at an atrial rate of eighty. It does not demonstrate progressive AV delay or distinguish nodal from infranodal block.

Infranodal block established by the wide QRS: A wide QRS increases concern for His–Purkinje disease but is not definitive localization. Bundle-branch disease can coexist with nodal block; additional clinical and physiological evidence may be needed.

questions.question: During supervised exercise evaluation of stable 2:1 AV block of uncertain level, the atrial rate increases and conduction deteriorates to 3:1 with reproduction of lightheadedness. The test is stopped and the patient is assessed promptly. Which interpretation best guides further management?
options: The response raises concern for infranodal conduction disease requiring urgent specialist pacing assessment
The response supports physiological vagal nodal block
The response establishes sinus chronotropic incompetence
The response establishes exercise-induced myocardial ischemia as the cause
questions.explanation:
Exercise Response and AV Block Localization

Correct answer: The response raises concern for infranodal conduction disease requiring urgent specialist pacing assessment

Use Physiology to Refine the Anatomical Hypothesis

**Exercise generally improves AV nodal conduction but may expose diseased His–Purkinje tissue as atrial impulses arrive faster.** Deterioration of conduction therefore supports concern for an infranodal site.

This is a clinically useful inference rather than direct histological proof. Integrate the QRS pattern, symptoms, structural findings, drug exposure and the actual exercise recording.

Improvement of an asymptomatic narrow-QRS 2:1 pattern, especially with accompanying Wenckebach, supports a supra-Hisian explanation. That reassuring scenario differs from symptomatic progression to a higher conduction ratio.

Prioritize Safety and Resolve Remaining Uncertainty

**Stop testing for clinically important symptomatic deterioration and arrange monitored assessment.** Exercise is a diagnostic tool for selected stable patients, not a stress challenge to continue through dangerous block.

EPS can define nodal, intra-Hisian or infra-Hisian disease when localization remains uncertain and will change management. Evaluate reversible causes and selected ischemic or inflammatory explanations according to the full presentation.

Confirmed nonreversible advanced infranodal disease supports permanent pacing; unstable patients may need temporary support while a definitive plan is made. Do not reassure solely because the resting strip had a modest ventricular rate or the patient was initially asymptomatic. Equally, do not assume that every exercise-associated symptom is conduction-related without a recorded association. The reproduced symptom with documented worsening block supplies the consequential link here.

The response supports physiological vagal nodal block: Vagally mediated nodal block commonly improves as vagal tone withdraws with exercise. Deterioration despite increasing sympathetic drive is concerning for a different mechanism, particularly when symptoms occur.

The response establishes sinus chronotropic incompetence: The sinus rate increases, while fewer atrial impulses reach the ventricles. The limitation is worsening AV conduction rather than inadequate sinus acceleration.

The response establishes exercise-induced myocardial ischemia as the cause: Ischemia can occasionally contribute to exercise-related conduction abnormalities and should be considered when supported by the presentation. Worsening block alone does not establish coronary ischemia rather than intrinsic infranodal disease.

Correct answer: High-grade AV block with three-to-one conduction

Count Atrial Impulses Before Naming the Pattern

**High-grade or advanced AV block includes two or more consecutive nonconducted sinus P waves with some remaining AV conduction.** The supplied 3:1 pattern meets that definition.

Confirm that the atrial rate is physiological and that the nonconducted deflections are sinus impulses rather than premature ectopy. Atrial tachycardia or flutter with a conduction ratio requires a different interpretation.

A slow ventricular rate alone cannot distinguish conducted responses from escape activity. Follow P-to-QRS timing over enough cycles to establish whether a causal conduction relationship exists.

Distinguish Severity From Exact Localization

**High-grade block is a concerning conduction finding even when every third impulse still reaches the ventricles.** The anatomical level and reversibility require assessment; the ratio alone does not provide them.

Assess perfusion, syncope, QRS pattern, drugs, electrolytes, ischemia and relevant inflammatory or infectious causes. Unstable bradycardia requires monitored resuscitation and pacing support as appropriate.

Nonreversible acquired high-grade AV block supports permanent pacing even without reported symptoms under the named US guideline. Temporary improvement in one recording does not establish durable recovery. Conversely, complete AV dissociation should not be assigned when clear conducted beats remain. Communicate both the atrial/ventricular rates and observed conduction pattern so urgency is understood without overstating the degree or anatomical certainty.

2:1 AV block | Every second sinus P conducts

High-grade AV block | At least two consecutive P waves blocked; some conduction remains

Complete AV block | No demonstrated AV conduction; subsidiary ventricular activation

SA exit block | Expected atrial activation is absent rather than a visible P failing to conduct

Complete AV block with an escape rhythm at thirty per minute: Complete block has no effective atrioventricular conduction. Here each ventricular response is demonstrably conducted from a sinus P wave with a reproducible PR, so residual conduction remains.

Two-to-one AV block: A 2:1 pattern blocks alternate P waves and conducts every second impulse. The supplied record blocks two successive impulses and conducts the third, establishing a 3:1 rather than 2:1 relationship.

Second-degree sinoatrial exit block: SA exit block produces failure of expected atrial activation. Sinus P waves continue regularly here; the failure occurs between atrial and ventricular activation rather than before the visible P wave.

questions.question: A stable patient has sinus P waves at 58/min and a narrow-QRS junctional rhythm at 62/min, with varying P–QRS relationships. During observation, the sinus rate increases to 78/min and one-to-one conduction resumes with PR 170 ms. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Interference AV dissociation with demonstrable preserved AV conduction
Persistent complete AV block
Two-to-one AV block
Sinus arrest with junctional escape
questions.explanation:
AV Dissociation Without Persistent Complete Heart Block

Correct answer: Interference AV dissociation with demonstrable preserved AV conduction

AV Dissociation Describes Independence, Not One Etiology

**Atria and ventricles may be activated independently when a subsidiary rhythm competes with the sinus node, even if the AV conduction system can conduct.** This is interference dissociation rather than proof of complete block.

A slowing sinus rhythm or accelerated junctional/ventricular focus can create this pattern. Similar atrial and ventricular rates can produce shifting apparent PR relationships.

The return of one-to-one sinus conduction as the atrial rate increases demonstrates preserved conduction at that time. Do not describe that finding as exclusion of every possible intermittent conduction disorder.

Identify What Is Driving the Competing Rhythms

**Compare atrial and ventricular rates, QRS morphology, timing and any capture of ventricular activation by sinus impulses.** Examine a sufficiently long strip rather than treating one dissociated snapshot as a complete diagnosis.

Review drugs, autonomic state, ischemia and other causes of subsidiary-rhythm acceleration or sinus slowing. Wide-complex tachycardia with AV dissociation creates a different urgent diagnostic context from this stable narrow-QRS rhythm.

A permanent pacemaker should not be chosen merely because the words AV dissociation appear on a tracing report. Treat an established cause or independently documented pacing indication. New syncope, progressive conduction abnormalities or recurrent unexplained pauses can still justify monitoring and further assessment. Document the evidence for actual block separately from the observation that atrial and ventricular activation were temporarily independent.

Persistent complete AV block: The dissociated segment can resemble complete block, but subsequent ordinary one-to-one sinus conduction establishes that persistent complete interruption is not present. Intermittent disease would require separate evidence.

Two-to-one AV block: A 2:1 pattern requires alternate sinus impulses conducting to the ventricles. The initial segment instead has a slightly faster independent junctional rhythm and no fixed alternate conduction relationship.

Sinus arrest with junctional escape: Sinus arrest would lack continuing sinus atrial depolarizations during the pause. Regular sinus P waves remain visible here; their rate is temporarily slower than the competing junctional rhythm.

ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia and conduction-delay guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628

ESC cardiac pacing and resynchronization guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: A young adult has an incidental nocturnal rhythm event without symptoms. Before transient AV block, sinus P–P intervals lengthen and conducted PR intervals prolong; both normalize as the sinus rate recovers. Daytime ECG, exercise conduction and echocardiography are normal. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: Sinus arrest
Intrinsic paroxysmal His–Purkinje block
Blocked atrial premature activity
Transient vagally mediated AV nodal block
questions.explanation:
Vagally Mediated AV Block

Correct answer: Transient vagally mediated AV nodal block

Look for Coordinated Sinus and AV Nodal Effects

**Increased vagal activity can slow sinus discharge and AV nodal conduction together.** Sinus slowing around the onset of AV block is a useful clue when interpreted with the whole recording.

The event can appear high-grade or even transiently complete, yet its physiological cause differs from persistent intrinsic conduction-system disease. Assess timing, triggers, QRS pattern, medications and structural findings.

Sleep-associated events also warrant a sleep-disordered-breathing history when clinically indicated. Do not assign the mechanism merely because an event occurred at night; the accompanying atrial and AV behavior matters.

Separate Incidental Events From Symptomatic Reflex Syncope

**Asymptomatic convincingly vagally mediated AV block does not warrant permanent pacing under the US 2018 framework.** This differs from nonreversible intrinsic advanced block.

Recurrent symptomatic reflex syncope requires a separate assessment of documented asystole, hypotensive susceptibility, age, injury risk and treatment options. A pacemaker may not correct the vasodepressor component even when bradycardia contributes.

The supplied normal daytime and exercise assessment supports conservative clinical follow-up. New unexplained syncope or worsening baseline conduction should reopen the diagnosis. Avoid treating one autonomic clue as absolute exclusion of coexisting disease, but also avoid converting an incidental physiological pattern into a prognostic pacing indication. Accurate symptom history and a verified tracing prevent both errors.

Sinus arrest: Sinus arrest produces absent atrial activation during the pause. Visible P waves fail to conduct in the described event, establishing an AV component in addition to the accompanying sinus slowing.

Intrinsic paroxysmal His–Purkinje block: Intrinsic paroxysmal block can cause abrupt dangerous ventricular pauses, often in a substrate of conduction disease. The coordinated sinus slowing and nodal delay around this transient event support an autonomic mechanism instead.

Blocked atrial premature activity: Blocked ectopy requires premature atrial activation, often with changed morphology or a P wave hidden in the preceding T wave. Here atrial intervals lengthen rather than an early ectopic impulse initiating the pause.

questions.question: A patient has recurrent unexplained syncope, right bundle-branch block with left anterior fascicular block and preserved LV function. Electrophysiology study shows a baseline HV interval of 78 ms. No reversible cause or competing established diagnosis is found. Under ESC 2021 guidance, which strategy is appropriate?
options: Repeat EPS only if the baseline HV reaches one hundred milliseconds
Insert a loop recorder and defer pacing until spontaneous complete block is captured
Recommend permanent pacemaker implantation
Implant an ICD on the basis of the prolonged HV interval
questions.explanation:
Syncope With Bifascicular Block and a Prolonged HV Interval

Correct answer: Recommend permanent pacemaker implantation

Use the Correct Electrophysiological Boundary

**ESC 2021 indicates pacing in unexplained syncope with bifascicular block when baseline HV is ==≥70 ms== or other qualifying intra-/infra-Hisian block is demonstrated.** The measured 78 ms meets that criterion.

HV measures conduction from His activation to ventricular activation. Prolongation indicates disease distal to the AV node and helps identify risk of intermittent advanced block.

Induced second- or third-degree intra-/infra-Hisian block during atrial pacing or an abnormal pharmacological challenge can also establish a positive study. Do not interchange baseline and provoked thresholds.

Understand What a Negative Study Would Mean

**A negative EPS does not exclude intermittent arrhythmic syncope.** Continued monitoring, often with an implantable recorder, may be appropriate when uncertainty remains after a negative study.

Selected older patients with recurrent unpredictable traumatic syncope may be considered for empirical pacing after individualized assessment. This is different from the positive-study indication already present here.

Assess alternative syncope mechanisms as well because hypotension and reflex susceptibility can coexist with conduction disease. Pacing can address intermittent block without guaranteeing elimination of every faint. Before implantation, review atrial rhythm, anticipated pacing burden, ventricular function and any independent ICD indication. Explain procedural risks and follow-up while avoiding a delay that requires another injury before acting on the documented high-risk substrate.

Repeat EPS only if the baseline HV reaches one hundred milliseconds: One hundred milliseconds is not the baseline threshold in the named syncope framework. Waiting for that value would miss patients meeting the baseline 70-ms criterion; pharmacological-challenge interpretation is a separate context.

Insert a loop recorder and defer pacing until spontaneous complete block is captured: An implantable recorder can be valuable after a nondiagnostic evaluation or negative EPS. The supplied prolonged HV meets the guideline’s positive electrophysiological criterion in syncope with bifascicular block, so another spontaneous event is not required.

Implant an ICD on the basis of the prolonged HV interval: An ICD is selected for a separate ventricular arrhythmia or sudden-death indication. Prolonged His–ventricular conduction identifies a pacing problem, not by itself a defibrillation indication in this preserved-LV presentation.

ESC cardiac pacing and resynchronization guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: A 35-year-old man with ongoing ischemic chest discomfort has new J-point elevation confined to V2 and V3, without LVH or bundle branch block. Which minimum elevation in both leads meets the standard age- and sex-specific threshold?
options: 2.0 mm
1.0 mm
1.5 mm
2.5 mm
questions.explanation:
Lead-Specific ST-Elevation Thresholds

Correct answer: 2.5 mm

Apply the Correct Lead and Patient Category

**In V2–V3, men younger than forty require at least 2.5 mm**, compared with 2 mm in older men and 1.5 mm in women.

Use the J-point and contiguous leads. The ordinary 1-mm threshold for other leads must not replace the V2–V3 qualification.

The standard framework assumes the absence of confounding LVH or bundle branch block, as specified in this stem.

Use the ECG to Direct Timely Clinical Assessment

**Thresholds support a working reperfusion diagnosis in the appropriate presentation**, not a complete etiologic diagnosis from voltage alone.

Evaluate symptom timing, prior tracings and reciprocal or evolving changes. Some acute occlusions do not display conventional qualifying elevation, and some nonischemic conditions do.

Do not wait for biomarkers to become positive when the presentation warrants emergency reperfusion assessment. Conversely, an isolated voltage criterion should be interpreted with its clinical context and the possibility of repolarization variants or other causes. Correct electrode placement and calibration matter when measurements sit near a boundary. The teaching point is a precise standard criterion, while the bedside decision remains an integrated assessment of possible acute coronary occlusion.

Lead group | Standard J-point threshold

V2–V3, men <40 years | ≥2.5 mm

V2–V3, men ≥40 years | ≥2.0 mm

V2–V3, women | ≥1.5 mm

Other standard leads | ≥1 mm in the required contiguous distribution

2.0 mm: Two millimeters is the V2–V3 threshold for men aged forty or older; the stated patient is thirty-five.

1.0 mm: One millimeter is the standard threshold in other qualifying leads, but V2–V3 require the specified age- and sex-specific threshold.

1.5 mm: One and a half millimeters is the V2–V3 threshold for women, not a man younger than forty.

Joint ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF Fifth Universal Definition of MI, 2026 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13523810/

bullets.text: **Thresholds support a working reperfusion diagnosis in the appropriate presentation**, not a complete etiologic diagnosis from voltage alone.

questions.question: A patient with ongoing ischemic discomfort has horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with prominent anterior R waves. No conventional ST-elevation territory is apparent. Which additional lead set most directly evaluates the suspected missed infarct?
options: Repeat limb leads with emphasis on aVR
Right-sided leads V3R–V4R
Posterior leads V7–V9
Repeat standard V1–V3 after moving them superiorly
questions.explanation:
Posterior Infarction Hidden in Anterior Reciprocal Changes

Correct answer: Posterior leads V7–V9

Interpret the Reciprocal View

**Posterior injury may appear as ST depression in anterior leads**, often with a prominent R wave as the reciprocal counterpart of a posterior Q-wave pattern.

Posterior V7–V9 recordings directly sample the suspected territory. The ESC 2023 supplementary ECG framework identifies elevation of at least 0.5 mm in V7–V9 as supporting posterior STEMI in the compatible clinical setting; standard anterior-lead thresholds should not be substituted for this posterior criterion.

Prominent anterior R waves have other causes, so the acute symptoms and ST pattern are necessary context rather than proof from R-wave height alone.

Act on the Integrated Occlusion Assessment

**A standard twelve-lead ECG can miss a posterior elevation pattern.** Additional leads should be acquired promptly while urgent coronary assessment proceeds.

Posterior infarction may accompany inferior or lateral involvement; do not force an isolated territory when the full tracing shows more extensive injury.

Serial ECGs, symptoms and hemodynamics remain important. A nondiagnostic initial biomarker does not remove concern during an early ongoing ischemic presentation. Distinguish this pattern from diffuse subendocardial ischemia and other causes of anterior depression using the full ECG and clinical evidence. Record electrode placement and acquisition time so the posterior tracing can be compared correctly. The useful next test is the lead set that resolves the suspected blind spot, not a delay for unrelated investigations.

Repeat limb leads with emphasis on aVR: Limb leads can clarify other ischemic patterns, but the described anterior reciprocal changes specifically call for posterior recording rather than aVR-focused assessment.

Right-sided leads V3R–V4R: Right-sided leads assess RV involvement, particularly with inferior infarction; they do not directly test the posterior territory suggested by anterior reciprocal depression.

Repeat standard V1–V3 after moving them superiorly: High right-precordial placement has other uses, but does not substitute for posterior leads in evaluating the suspected posterior injury pattern.

questions.question: A patient with inferior ST elevation develops hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure and relatively clear lungs. Which additional ECG recording most directly evaluates the suspected accompanying chamber involvement?
options: Repeat standard V5 and V6 at the same positions
Posterior leads V7–V9
Right precordial leads V3R and V4R
High right-precordial V1 and V2 recordings
questions.explanation:
Right Ventricular Involvement in Inferior Infarction

Correct answer: Right precordial leads V3R and V4R

Localize the Hemodynamic Problem

**Inferior infarction can involve the RV**, producing impaired forward delivery, venous congestion and hypotension without prominent pulmonary edema.

ESC guidance recommends right precordial recording in suspected inferior STEMI. Elevation in V3R–V4R supports ongoing RV ischemia.

The examination pattern is suggestive rather than exclusive; assess other causes of hypotension and obtain appropriate echo when useful.

Support Perfusion While Arranging Reperfusion

**Avoid reflex preload reduction in a hypotensive patient with suspected RV involvement.** Evaluate nitrate exposure, filling, rhythm and perfusion before treatment.

Fluid may help selected underfilled patients but should be titrated with reassessment; indiscriminate large-volume loading can worsen RV dilation and congestion.

Treat important bradycardia or AV dyssynchrony and maintain an urgent coronary reperfusion strategy. Clear lungs do not prove that every hypotensive patient needs fluid, just as venous distension does not independently establish the infarct territory. Record right-sided leads promptly because changes can evolve. The purpose of the additional tracing is to clarify a management-relevant extension of the infarct, not delay definitive care while seeking a perfect localization label.

Repeat standard V5 and V6 at the same positions: Lateral leads may show additional infarct extension, but do not replace right-sided leads for evaluating the suspected RV territory.

Posterior leads V7–V9: Posterior leads evaluate posterior injury and are useful with compatible reciprocal changes, but the hemodynamic pattern here specifically raises concern for RV involvement.

High right-precordial V1 and V2 recordings: High right-precordial placement can clarify selected electrical patterns, but the appropriate infarction assessment is a standard right-sided lead recording rather than a superior shift.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

questions.question: A patient with established LBBB has persistent ischemic discomfort. A predominantly negative QRS lead has an S-wave depth of 8 mm and discordant J-point elevation of 3 mm. Which interpretation is appropriate?
options: The finding requires at least 5 mm elevation as well as a qualifying ST/S ratio
The finding falls below the excessive-discordance threshold because elevation is under 5 mm
The finding falls below the proportional threshold because ST/S is less than positive 0.25
The discordance meets the proportional modified Sgarbossa criterion and supports urgent occlusion assessment
questions.explanation:
Proportionally Excessive Discordance in LBBB

Correct answer: The discordance meets the proportional modified Sgarbossa criterion and supports urgent occlusion assessment

Use the Sign Convention Correctly

**With an S wave recorded as −8 mm, the ST/S ratio is 3/−8 = −0.375.** This is at or below the −0.25 proportional boundary.

Equivalently, elevation is 37.5% of the S-wave magnitude, exceeding a quarter. The elevation also exceeds the minimum 1 mm used in the modified criterion.

This replaces the older fixed excessive-discordance threshold; it does not mean every expected discordant ST segment is abnormal.

Modified Sgarbossa Criteria

**The modified rule is positive when any one of three components is present:** concordant ST elevation at least 1 mm in a lead with a positive QRS; concordant ST depression at least 1 mm in V1, V2 or V3; or discordant elevation at least 1 mm with signed ST/S ratio at most −0.25.

Check baseline, calibration and lead quality. A negative criterion does not exclude occlusion in a patient with compelling ongoing ischemia.

Use urgent specialist assessment and appropriate reperfusion planning when the integrated picture is concerning. Do not delay necessary care while waiting for a biomarker rise, and do not infer that a positive criterion identifies the exact culprit artery. The original study supports improved detection with proportional assessment, but no ECG rule is perfectly sensitive or specific. Document the measured elevation, S-wave depth and clinical context so the interpretation can be reviewed rather than reduced to LBBB-positive or LBBB-negative.

The finding requires at least 5 mm elevation as well as a qualifying ST/S ratio: The modified proportional criterion requires at least one millimeter of discordant elevation, not a second five-millimeter requirement; three millimeters satisfies the amplitude component.

The finding falls below the excessive-discordance threshold because elevation is under 5 mm: Five millimeters is the original absolute discordance boundary; the modified criterion instead identifies disproportionate elevation relative to S-wave depth, which this lead satisfies.

The finding falls below the proportional threshold because ST/S is less than positive 0.25: The signed ratio uses a negative S-wave amplitude and is compared with minus 0.25 or lower; alternatively compare positive magnitudes, where 37.5 percent exceeds twenty-five percent.

Smith et al. modified Sgarbossa derivation study, 2012 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22939607/

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

questions.question: A patient has persistent crushing chest discomfort. ECG shows upsloping J-point depression across the precordial leads merging into tall symmetric T waves, without conventional anterior ST elevation. Potassium is normal. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Repeat ECGs until conventional anterior elevation appears before activating the pathway
Use serial troponin results to decide whether to activate the emergency invasive pathway
Plan inpatient angiography within twenty-four hours after initial medical stabilization
Arrange emergency coronary occlusion assessment and reperfusion planning
questions.explanation:
de Winter Pattern During Ongoing Ischemic Pain

Correct answer: Arrange emergency coronary occlusion assessment and reperfusion planning

Recognize Occlusion Without Conventional Elevation

**The de Winter pattern combines precordial upsloping depression with prominent symmetric T waves.** It was described in acute LAD occlusion.

Interpret the pattern with the ongoing symptoms, prior tracing and the full ECG. It is not simply a large T wave or an isolated numerical amplitude criterion.

Hyperacute ischemic T waves and evolving occlusion patterns may change over time; obtain serial recordings without delaying escalation.

Do Not Wait for a More Familiar Pattern

**Persistent ischemia with an occlusion-suggestive ECG requires urgent coronary assessment.** Biomarker negativity early after symptom onset does not remove this concern.

Check important mimics such as electrolyte abnormalities in parallel, but do not use a pending test as a reason to postpone necessary care.

The pattern is associated with LAD disease but should not be presented as a perfectly specific map of the culprit in every patient. Definitive anatomy and treatment follow the emergency assessment. Communicate the concern clearly to the receiving team rather than describing the ECG merely as nonspecific ST depression. A working occlusion diagnosis is meant to accelerate an appropriate reperfusion pathway, not to require that every feature of a textbook image be present before action.

Repeat ECGs until conventional anterior elevation appears before activating the pathway: Serial ECGs help identify evolving ischemia and should continue during care, but waiting for conventional elevation can delay reperfusion when the current pattern already suggests occlusion.

Use serial troponin results to decide whether to activate the emergency invasive pathway: Serial biomarkers are appropriate in many stable suspected ACS presentations, but persistent ischemia with this occlusion-suggestive pattern warrants escalation before biochemical confirmation.

Plan inpatient angiography within twenty-four hours after initial medical stabilization: An early inpatient approach suits selected stable high-risk NSTE-ACS, but ongoing pain with an occlusion-suggestive ECG requires more immediate assessment than that planned interval.

questions.question: During ongoing chest discomfort, a patient has horizontal ST depression in multiple inferolateral leads with ST elevation in aVR. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Acute left-main coronary thrombosis established from the ECG
A high-risk global ischemic pattern that requires clinical assessment without uniquely identifying left-main occlusion
Severe three-vessel coronary disease established from the ECG
Secondary ischemia from a systemic supply–demand trigger established from the ECG
questions.explanation:
Diffuse ST Depression With aVR Elevation

Correct answer: A high-risk global ischemic pattern that requires clinical assessment without uniquely identifying left-main occlusion

Describe the Ischemic Pattern Before the Anatomy

**Widespread ST depression with aVR elevation can reflect global subendocardial ischemia.** Left-main or multivessel coronary disease belongs in the differential.

The same appearance can occur during severe supply–demand imbalance and other presentations. The ECG does not independently establish acute left-main thrombosis.

Evaluate symptoms, blood pressure, rhythm, oxygenation and the extent and evolution of changes.

Let Instability and Persistent Ischemia Determine Urgency

**Hemodynamic compromise or refractory symptoms require urgent escalation.** A high-risk pattern should not be placed in a low-risk pathway merely because regional elevation is absent.

Treat a reversible trigger when present while reassessing whether an acute primary coronary process remains plausible. Persistent changes after correction warrant continued concern.

Use the full clinical evidence to plan invasive assessment and antithrombotic treatment, considering important alternative emergencies and bleeding risk. A precise handover distinguishes the observed ECG from an unconfirmed anatomic diagnosis. Avoid the opposite errors of overcalling one specific lesion and underreacting to a potentially extensive ischemic burden. Serial comparison can clarify evolution, but observation should not delay intervention when the patient is unstable.

Acute left-main coronary thrombosis established from the ECG: Left-main disease is an important possibility, but this appearance does not distinguish acute thrombosis from severe multivessel disease or global supply–demand ischemia without further assessment.

Severe three-vessel coronary disease established from the ECG: Multivessel disease can cause this pattern, but angiographic anatomy cannot be determined definitively from the ECG; an acute left-main process and systemic mismatch remain alternatives.

Secondary ischemia from a systemic supply–demand trigger established from the ECG: Severe anemia, hypoxemia or hemodynamic stress can produce global ischemia, but the tracing alone does not establish such a trigger or exclude a primary acute coronary process.

explanationTeaching.title: Diffuse ST Depression With aVR Elevation

sections.heading: Describe the Ischemic Pattern Before the Anatomy

bullets.text: **Widespread ST depression with aVR elevation can reflect global subendocardial ischemia.** Left-main or multivessel coronary disease belongs in the differential.
children: The same appearance can occur during severe supply–demand imbalance and other presentations. The ECG does not independently establish acute left-main thrombosis.
Evaluate symptoms, blood pressure, rhythm, oxygenation and the extent and evolution of changes.

sections.heading: Let Instability and Persistent Ischemia Determine Urgency

bullets.text: **Hemodynamic compromise or refractory symptoms require urgent escalation.** A high-risk pattern should not be placed in a low-risk pathway merely because regional elevation is absent.
children: Treat a reversible trigger when present while reassessing whether an acute primary coronary process remains plausible. Persistent changes after correction warrant continued concern.

Use the full clinical evidence to plan invasive assessment and antithrombotic treatment, considering important alternative emergencies and bleeding risk. A precise handover distinguishes the observed ECG from an unconfirmed anatomic diagnosis. Avoid the opposite errors of overcalling one specific lesion and underreacting to a potentially extensive ischemic burden. Serial comparison can clarify evolution, but observation should not delay intervention when the patient is unstable.

otherOptions.explanation: Left-main disease is an important possibility, but this appearance does not distinguish acute thrombosis from severe multivessel disease or global supply–demand ischemia without further assessment.
Multivessel disease can cause this pattern, but angiographic anatomy cannot be determined definitively from the ECG; an acute left-main process and systemic mismatch remain alternatives.
Severe anemia, hypoxemia or hemodynamic stress can produce global ischemia, but the tracing alone does not establish such a trigger or exclude a primary acute coronary process.

questions.question: A patient has repeated episodes of ischemic discomfort with transient ST elevation that resolves between attacks. Pain and ECG changes recur despite initial treatment. Under the 2023 ESC ACS framework, which approach is appropriate?
options: Immediate invasive assessment for recurrent ischemia with dynamic ECG changes
Arrange early inpatient angiography within twenty-four hours after serial biomarker assessment
Continue medical treatment and reserve angiography for persistent ST elevation
Begin a calcium antagonist trial and defer angiography until the symptom response is assessed
questions.explanation:
Recurrent Transient ST Elevation Is Not a Reassuring Resolution

Correct answer: Immediate invasive assessment for recurrent ischemia with dynamic ECG changes

Distinguish Resolved High-Risk Features From Ongoing Instability

**Recurrent or refractory ischemia and repeated dynamic ECG changes support an immediate invasive strategy.** A normalized tracing between attacks does not erase the clinical sequence.

A stable patient after one resolved transient episode has a different risk context from this patient with recurrence despite treatment.

Document ECGs during symptoms and after resolution rather than using only the latest apparently improved tracing.

Escalate While Continuing Monitored Care

**Continue rhythm and hemodynamic monitoring and urgent cardiology coordination.** Reassess the mechanism and treatment response while arranging definitive evaluation.

Troponin adds information about injury but does not need to become positive before persistent high-risk ischemia is addressed.

The distinction between immediate and early assessment depends on the current clinical state, not simply an isolated score or an ECG label. If a vasomotor mechanism is eventually established, tailor treatment accordingly; do not presume it from nitrate response or transient changes alone. Communicate recurrent episodes clearly at handover so that an asymptomatic interval is not mistaken for a low-risk presentation. The purpose of serial evaluation is to detect this evolving risk and act on it, rather than collect additional normal intervals while ischemia continues.

Arrange early inpatient angiography within twenty-four hours after serial biomarker assessment: An early inpatient strategy suits stable high-risk features, but recurrent ischemia despite treatment with repeated dynamic changes supports immediate assessment without waiting for biomarker confirmation.

Continue medical treatment and reserve angiography for persistent ST elevation: Persistent elevation identifies a familiar emergency pathway, but repeated transient elevation during refractory ischemia is itself a very-high-risk feature; waiting for persistence can delay indicated intervention.

Begin a calcium antagonist trial and defer angiography until the symptom response is assessed: Calcium antagonists are appropriate for established vasospastic angina, but reversibility alone does not establish spasm; a treatment trial should not postpone assessment of this recurrent unstable presentation.

questions.question: A patient has sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward, a friction rub, widespread ST elevation and PR depression. There is no territorial reciprocal depression apart from expected changes in aVR. Which diagnosis best fits the integrated presentation?
options: A persistent post-infarct ventricular aneurysm pattern
Acute territorial coronary occlusion
Benign early repolarization
Acute pericarditis
questions.explanation:
Pericarditis Versus a Territorial Coronary Pattern

Correct answer: Acute pericarditis

Integrate the Symptoms and Examination With the ECG

**Widespread elevation with PR depression supports pericarditis in the appropriate inflammatory presentation.** The rub and positional pleuritic pain provide independent clinical evidence.

ST shape alone is insufficient: concavity does not reliably exclude coronary occlusion, and inflammatory disease can occasionally produce regional findings.

Under ESC 2025, a definite clinical pericarditis diagnosis requires a compatible presentation with more than one additional criterion; one supports possible pericarditis. This stem supplies both a rub and characteristic ECG changes. These are separate criteria; PR depression and widespread elevation are components of the same ECG category, not two independent categories.

Assess Extent and Complications

**Obtain appropriate echocardiography, inflammatory markers and myocardial-injury assessment.** Effusion, ventricular dysfunction or elevated troponin can change the evaluation.

Consider myocardial involvement and important alternative causes when the presentation is atypical or severe. A pericarditis diagnosis does not imply that coronary disease cannot coexist.

If coronary occlusion remains plausible, resolve it urgently. Assess tamponade, significant effusion, myocardial involvement and secondary causes before disposition. Elevated troponin suggests associated myocardial injury rather than providing an additional pericarditis biomarker criterion. Treatment and follow-up depend on this full assessment, not ST morphology alone.

Additional pericarditis criterion: ESC 2025 | Finding

Examination | Pericardial friction rub

ECG | PR depression or widespread ST elevation

Inflammatory biomarker | Raised CRP

Echocardiography | New or worsening pericardial effusion

CMR | Pericardial edema or late gadolinium enhancement

A persistent post-infarct ventricular aneurysm pattern: An aneurysm can produce persistent regional ST elevation after an infarct, usually with supporting history and Q-wave or imaging evidence; it does not match the acute widespread inflammatory pattern here.

Acute territorial coronary occlusion: Coronary occlusion remains an important alternative in chest pain, but the positional pleuritic symptoms, rub and widespread PR/ST pattern favor pericardial inflammation rather than one coronary territory.

Benign early repolarization: Early repolarization can cause widespread elevation, but does not explain a new friction rub and the stated inflammatory pain pattern as well as acute pericarditis.
