questions.question: After recurrent chest pain has resolved, ECG shows deeply symmetric T-wave inversion in V2–V4 with preserved R waves and no substantial ST elevation. Troponin is not markedly elevated. What is the best next strategy?
options: Routine outpatient review because pain has resolved
Exercise treadmill testing to confirm inducible ischemia
Urgent coronary evaluation while avoiding provocative exercise testing
Diagnose prior completed anterior infarction solely from T inversion
questions.explanation:
Wellens Pattern During a Pain-Free Interval

Correct answer: Urgent coronary evaluation while avoiding provocative exercise testing

Pattern and Context

**Biphasic or deep symmetric anterior T inversion after pain resolves** is a high-risk reperfusion/ischemic pattern.

A severe LAD lesion is a classic association; normal or mildly elevated biomarkers do not exclude it.

Action and Differential

**Urgent ACS/coronary assessment** is appropriate; avoid an exercise stress challenge.

**Consider mimics** such as LVH, pulmonary embolism, CNS injury or cardiomyopathy when the clinical context differs.

ECG morphology supports a pathway but does not by itself establish exact coronary anatomy; use serial ECGs and definitive assessment.

Routine outpatient review because pain has resolved: Wellens changes commonly appear when pain-free and can signal a high-risk LAD lesion; symptom resolution does not justify delayed assessment.

Exercise treadmill testing to confirm inducible ischemia: Provocative stress can precipitate infarction in a Wellens-type high-risk coronary pattern; a low troponin does not establish safety.

Diagnose prior completed anterior infarction solely from T inversion: T inversion without pathological Q waves or loss of R progression does not prove a completed old infarct; the recent pain pattern suggests active coronary risk.

Fifth Universal Definition of MI, 2026 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.07.025

questions.question: A hemodynamically stable adult with positional pleuritic pain has widespread concave ST elevation and PR depression. Which additional ECG finding would most strongly increase concern for a coronary occlusion rather than uncomplicated pericarditis?
options: ST depression limited to aVR and V1
PR elevation in aVR
Reciprocal ST depression in aVL accompanying inferior ST elevation
Downsloping of the TP segment in multiple leads
questions.explanation:
Pericardial ECG Changes and Coronary Mimics

Correct answer: Reciprocal ST depression in aVL accompanying inferior ST elevation

Interpret Distribution Rather Than Shape Alone

**Widespread ST elevation with PR displacement supports pericardial inflammation, whereas a vascular-territory pattern with reciprocal changes favors ischemia.** No isolated ECG sign safely excludes an acute coronary occlusion.

Concave ST elevation can occur in early infarction. ST elevation in lead III exceeding lead II, reciprocal depression outside aVR or V1, evolving Q waves and corresponding regional dysfunction should increase ischemic concern.

Early repolarization can produce stable concave ST elevation and J-point notching, but does not itself explain new inflammatory pain, a rub or a rising inflammatory marker. Prior tracings and serial change can help.

Recognize the Limits of Classical Staging

**The traditional ST/PR, normalization, T-wave inversion and recovery sequence is not obligatory.** Treatment and timing can modify the observed ECG, and some patients never show the classical changes.

PR depression is not exclusive to pericarditis, and Spodick sign has also been observed with STEMI. Use these as contextual clues rather than diagnostic vetoes.

When symptoms or serial findings suggest ischemia, follow the urgent ACS pathway rather than waiting for a textbook pericarditis stage. Obtain troponin and echo as clinically indicated, recognizing that injury markers may rise in either infarction or inflammatory myocardial involvement. A normal or atypical tracing does not end the investigation when the clinical presentation remains concerning.

Pattern | Interpretation

Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression | Supports pericardial inflammation in the clinical context

Territorial ST elevation with reciprocal aVL depression | Raises concern for inferior coronary occlusion

Stable J-point notching on previous ECG | Supports a repolarization variant; does not explain new symptoms

TP downsloping | Supportive clue with limited specificity

ST depression limited to aVR and V1: These leads can show reciprocal ST depression in a diffuse pericardial pattern. Depression in other leads, especially a territorial reciprocal pattern, raises more concern for an ischemic explanation.

PR elevation in aVR: Reciprocal PR elevation in aVR can accompany atrial epicardial inflammation and diffuse PR depression in pericarditis. It does not carry the same implication as a territorial reciprocal ST pattern.

Downsloping of the TP segment in multiple leads: Spodick sign can support pericarditis, although it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to establish the diagnosis. It is less concerning for coronary occlusion than the supplied reciprocal aVL change.

Evaluation of Spodick sign and other ECG findings in STEMI and pericarditis, 2020 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jemermed.2020.01.017

questions.question: A patient with a large circumferential effusion has regular sinus tachycardia. Every QRS is preceded by a P wave; alternate QRS complexes differ in amplitude and axis, while QRS complexes remain narrow and RR intervals remain stable. Which mechanism best explains the ECG pattern?
options: Alternating His–Purkinje conduction block
Alternating strength of ventricular contraction
Alternating normal and premature ventricular beats
Movement of the heart within the fluid-filled pericardial sac
questions.explanation:
Electrical Alternans in a Large Pericardial Effusion

Correct answer: Movement of the heart within the fluid-filled pericardial sac

Relate the Electrical Vector to Cardiac Position

**A large effusion can permit pendular motion and rotation of the heart within the pericardial space.** The changing relation between myocardium and surface electrodes produces beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude or axis.

Low QRS voltage and sinus tachycardia can accompany the pattern. Their absence does not exclude an effusion, and neither low voltage nor tachycardia alone is specific for a pericardial cause.

First confirm lead stability, rhythm and the presence or absence of premature beats or changing conduction. Movement artefact and arrhythmia must not be mislabeled as a mechanical swinging-heart phenomenon.

Distinguish the ECG Clue From the Hemodynamic Diagnosis

**Electrical alternans raises concern for a substantial effusion and possible tamponade but does not establish the pressure effect by itself.** Assess perfusion and obtain urgent echocardiographic evaluation in the relevant clinical setting.

Mechanical pulsus alternans concerns alternating arterial pulse amplitude; pulsus paradoxus concerns respiratory systolic-pressure variation. These are different observations and can coexist without being interchangeable definitions.

Echo should assess the collection, chamber behavior and filling physiology, with attention to regional compression or altered loading. A large collection can be tolerated if it accumulates slowly, while a smaller rapidly accumulating collection can cause shock without the classic ECG. Drain promptly when clinical tamponade is established, using the route appropriate to the cause and anatomy. Do not wait for electrical alternans before treating a convincing unstable presentation, and do not perform drainage solely because an alternating ECG pattern appears without a causative compressive collection.

Observation | Distinguishing feature

Effusion-associated electrical alternans | Alternating surface QRS vector from changing cardiac position

Ventricular bigeminy | Premature ventricular activation and a characteristic timing pattern

Alternating bundle-branch conduction | Changing ventricular conduction morphology or duration

Mechanical pulsus alternans | Alternating arterial pulse strength; an ECG alternans pattern is not required

Alternating His–Purkinje conduction block: Alternating aberrancy or bundle-branch block can change QRS morphology and usually changes its width or conduction pattern. Here the stable narrow activation with amplitude and axis changes in a large effusion favors positional alternans.

Alternating strength of ventricular contraction: Mechanical pulsus alternans is beat-to-beat variation in arterial pulse strength and can occur in severe ventricular dysfunction. It does not by itself explain the alternating surface QRS vector in this effusion-associated pattern.

Alternating normal and premature ventricular beats: Ventricular bigeminy can create alternating QRS forms, but premature timing, different ventricular activation and coupling or compensatory-pause features help identify it. The supplied regular sinus activation and stable QRS duration do not support that explanation.

sections.heading: Relate the Electrical Vector to Cardiac Position

bullets.text: **A large effusion can permit pendular motion and rotation of the heart within the pericardial space.** The changing relation between myocardium and surface electrodes produces beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude or axis.
children: Low QRS voltage and sinus tachycardia can accompany the pattern. Their absence does not exclude an effusion, and neither low voltage nor tachycardia alone is specific for a pericardial cause.

First confirm lead stability, rhythm and the presence or absence of premature beats or changing conduction. Movement artefact and arrhythmia must not be mislabeled as a mechanical swinging-heart phenomenon.

sections.heading: Distinguish the ECG Clue From the Hemodynamic Diagnosis

bullets.text: **Electrical alternans raises concern for a substantial effusion and possible tamponade but does not establish the pressure effect by itself.** Assess perfusion and obtain urgent echocardiographic evaluation in the relevant clinical setting.
children: Mechanical pulsus alternans concerns alternating arterial pulse amplitude; pulsus paradoxus concerns respiratory systolic-pressure variation. These are different observations and can coexist without being interchangeable definitions.

Echo should assess the collection, chamber behavior and filling physiology, with attention to regional compression or altered loading. A large collection can be tolerated if it accumulates slowly, while a smaller rapidly accumulating collection can cause shock without the classic ECG. Drain promptly when clinical tamponade is established, using the route appropriate to the cause and anatomy. Do not wait for electrical alternans before treating a convincing unstable presentation, and do not perform drainage solely because an alternating ECG pattern appears without a causative compressive collection.

questions.question: During evaluation of palpitations, continuous ECG shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm gradually accelerating from 90 to 135/min as fever rises. P-wave morphology and axis match the baseline sinus tracing, and the rate falls gradually after treatment of fever and dehydration. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Physiological sinus tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Sinus Tachycardia Versus Paroxysmal Reentrant SVT

Correct answer: Physiological sinus tachycardia

Interpret the Whole Rate Trajectory

**Sinus tachycardia is usually a response to increased demand or altered autonomic drive.** Fever, hypovolemia, pain, hypoxemia, anemia, thyrotoxicosis and other triggers should be sought according to the presentation.

A sinus-appearing P wave before each QRS, appropriate atrial axis and gradual acceleration or deceleration support the diagnosis. Comparison with the baseline tracing is useful when morphology is uncertain.

Atrial and ventricular rates alone do not define the mechanism. Sinus tachycardia can be rapid, while AVNRT or AVRT can be relatively slow under medication or in older patients.

Treat the Driver Before Suppressing the Rate

**Correct the physiological cause and reassess perfusion and symptoms.** Tachycardia may be compensatory, so reflex AV-nodal blockade can worsen output in a depleted or critically ill patient.

Reentrant SVTs typically have abrupt onset and termination, whereas automatic focal AT may show warm-up and cool-down. These are clues that require integration with atrial morphology and a recorded episode.

Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is considered only when a persistent symptomatic sinus-rate syndrome is not explained by a physiological or secondary cause. A febrile dehydrated patient does not meet that interpretation simply because the resting rate exceeds 100/min. POTS requires a posture-related assessment and its own criteria rather than a fever-associated tracing. Obtain a 12-lead ECG during symptoms when feasible and reconsider the mechanism if episodes remain abrupt or unexplained after the trigger resolves.

Focal atrial tachycardia: An automatic atrial focus can warm up and cool down, so gradual change alone is not diagnostic. Here the unchanged sinus morphology and rate response to a documented physiological demand favor sinus tachycardia rather than a non-sinus focus.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: AVNRT commonly starts and stops abruptly and often obscures atrial activity within or near the QRS. Gradual rate change with a physiological trigger and unchanged sinus P waves supports sinus activation instead.

Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Orthodromic AVRT usually has abrupt paroxysms and retrograde atrial activation associated with a circuit using the AV node and an accessory pathway. The observed gradual sinus-rate trajectory is less consistent with that mechanism.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: A patient has abrupt recurrent regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 185/min. Retrograde atrial deflections appear just after the QRS with a very short RP interval. The baseline ECG has no delta wave. Which interpretation is most defensible before electrophysiological confirmation?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia is established by a visible atrial deflection
Orthodromic AVRT is excluded by the normal baseline ECG
Typical AVNRT is favored, but orthodromic AVRT through a concealed pathway remains possible
Typical atrial flutter is established by the ventricular rate
questions.explanation:
Short-RP Regular Narrow-Complex Tachycardia

Correct answer: Typical AVNRT is favored, but orthodromic AVRT through a concealed pathway remains possible

RP Timing Narrows the Differential

**A very short RP interval during abrupt regular SVT favors typical slow–fast AVNRT.** Near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation can hide retrograde P waves or produce a pseudo-r-prime in V1 or pseudo-S waves inferiorly.

Orthodromic AVRT uses antegrade AV nodal/His–Purkinje conduction and retrograde accessory-pathway conduction. Its retrograde P wave may also lie shortly after the QRS, so surface timing is not an infallible circuit diagnosis.

A concealed pathway conducts retrogradely without manifest antegrade pre-excitation. A normal sinus-rhythm ECG therefore cannot independently exclude accessory-pathway-mediated tachycardia.

Use the Recording to Guide Further Assessment

**Preserve a 12-lead tracing during tachycardia and compare it with sinus rhythm.** Examine regularity, QRS width, atrial activation and onset or termination rather than relying on a rate label.

Vagal maneuvers or adenosine can terminate AV-node-dependent circuits in a suitable stable patient. Termination supports nodal dependence but does not alone distinguish AVNRT from AVRT, and some focal tachycardias can also respond.

EPS can establish the mechanism when recurrent symptoms justify definitive assessment or ablation. Initial management still depends on hemodynamic stability and the actual rhythm: a diagnostic hypothesis must not delay treatment of attributable shock. Explain that the likely diagnosis can be clinically useful without pretending that a short-RP strip uniquely identifies every circuit. The eventual ablation target differs between an AV nodal slow pathway and an accessory pathway, making precise mechanism assessment consequential.

Focal atrial tachycardia is established by a visible atrial deflection: Visible atrial activity occurs in several SVTs, including retrograde activation during AVNRT or AVRT. Its timing, morphology and response to diagnostic maneuvers matter more than visibility alone.

Orthodromic AVRT is excluded by the normal baseline ECG: An accessory pathway that conducts only retrogradely can support orthodromic AVRT without producing a delta wave in sinus rhythm. Absence of manifest pre-excitation therefore does not exclude this circuit.

Typical atrial flutter is established by the ventricular rate: Flutter with 2:1 conduction often produces a rate near 150/min, but rates vary and rate alone is not diagnostic. The supplied tracing does not demonstrate a continuing flutter cycle or additional atrial waves.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: A stable patient has regular narrow-complex tachycardia with RP longer than PR and negative P waves in the inferior leads. Adenosine terminates the episode. Which conclusion is most defensible from these findings alone?
options: Negative inferior P waves establish permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia
Adenosine termination establishes atypical AVNRT
Atypical AVNRT, slowly conducting-pathway AVRT and adenosine-sensitive atrial tachycardia remain possible
RP longer than PR establishes focal atrial tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Long-RP Supraventricular Tachycardia

Correct answer: Atypical AVNRT, slowly conducting-pathway AVRT and adenosine-sensitive atrial tachycardia remain possible

Delayed Atrial Timing Has Several Mechanisms

**Long-RP tachycardia describes atrial activation late after the preceding QRS, with RP longer than the following PR.** It does not by itself establish whether atrial activity drives or follows the ventricular cycle.

Fast–slow or slow–slow AVNRT can have delayed retrograde nodal activation. PJRT is orthodromic AVRT using a slowly conducting, decremental retrograde accessory pathway, commonly producing inferiorly negative P waves.

A focal atrial source can produce a similar apparent relationship. Sinus tachycardia and other junctional mechanisms remain relevant in the appropriate clinical context; onset, offset and atrial morphology help refine the assessment.

Adenosine Response Is Not a Mechanism Label

**Adenosine termination is compatible with more than one long-RP circuit.** AV-node-dependent reentry can stop, while certain adenosine-sensitive focal atrial mechanisms can also terminate.

Record the full termination sequence and determine whether atrial activity persists when ventricular conduction is interrupted. EPS can resolve the mechanism when recurrent symptoms or an ablation decision make certainty consequential.

Incessant long-RP tachycardia can cause tachycardia-mediated ventricular dysfunction, particularly with PJRT or incessant AT. Evaluate burden and ventricular function rather than assuming a modest rate makes it harmless. Treatment and ablation targets differ between a slow nodal pathway, an accessory pathway and an atrial focus. Avoid applying a definitive procedural label from one P-wave polarity or an adenosine response; preserve the working differential until sufficient evidence is available.

Mechanism | Reason for long RP | Important qualification

Atypical AVNRT | Delayed retrograde nodal activation | Inferiorly negative P waves can resemble PJRT

PJRT | Slow decremental retrograde accessory pathway | No baseline delta wave is required

Focal AT | Atrial focus with its own activation timing | Some forms terminate with adenosine

Negative inferior P waves establish permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia: PJRT often has long RP and inferiorly negative retrograde P waves, but atypical AVNRT and low atrial foci can resemble this pattern. Additional electrophysiological evidence is needed before assigning that specific pathway mechanism.

Adenosine termination establishes atypical AVNRT: Atypical AVNRT can terminate with adenosine, but slowly conducting accessory-pathway AVRT and some focal AT mechanisms can do so as well. The drug response is not a unique circuit identifier.

RP longer than PR establishes focal atrial tachycardia: Focal AT is an important long-RP diagnosis, but delayed retrograde conduction during atypical AVNRT or AVRT can produce the same surface timing relationship. RP classification narrows rather than completes the differential.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: During a regular narrow-complex tachycardia, adenosine causes several nonconducted atrial impulses. Discrete abnormal P waves continue at the same cycle length, separated by an isoelectric baseline, and one-to-one ventricular conduction then resumes. Which interpretation best fits the observed response?
options: An atrial tachycardia continuing independently of transient AV nodal block
Orthodromic AVRT continuing through the blocked AV node
Sinus tachycardia established by adenosine resistance
Typical AVNRT established by resumption of one-to-one conduction
questions.explanation:
Adenosine Unmasks Continuing Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: An atrial tachycardia continuing independently of transient AV nodal block

Inspect the Atria During the Ventricular Pause

**Adenosine can reveal atrial activity by transiently reducing AV conduction.** A continuing organized atrial rhythm may become visible when fewer QRS complexes obscure it.

Discrete abnormal P waves with intervening isoelectric segments support focal AT in the appropriate context. Flutter can also persist during AV block, but typically shows a macroreentrant atrial pattern; surface appearance is not infallible, especially with scar-related rhythms.

The atrial cycle length and activation pattern provide the diagnostic information. Merely observing a short ventricular pause or a lower displayed heart rate does not prove that the tachycardia terminated.

Interpret AV Block With Appropriate Limits

**Ordinary orthodromic AVRT needs antegrade conduction through the AV node.** Interruption usually stops that circuit, whereas an atrial rhythm can continue and later regain ventricular conduction.

AVNRT can occasionally persist despite block in an output pathway, so ventricular block by itself is not an absolute exclusion of every nodal circuit. Integrate the atrial recording, timing and other electrophysiological evidence.

Some focal ATs terminate with adenosine; others merely become easier to identify. Preserve the diagnostic strip and choose subsequent treatment according to the actual rhythm, symptoms, burden and ventricular function. Do not repeatedly escalate adenosine simply because a continuing atrial rhythm fails to terminate. For recurrent or incessant symptomatic focal AT, specialist evaluation and ablation can be appropriate. Acute hemodynamic compromise still requires immediate rhythm-directed management rather than prolonged diagnostic drug challenges.

Orthodromic AVRT continuing through the blocked AV node: The AV node is the antegrade limb of ordinary orthodromic AVRT. Sustained atrial activity at an unchanged cycle despite interruption of that limb argues against this circuit as the explanation.

Sinus tachycardia established by adenosine resistance: Sinus activity can continue during transient AV block, but adenosine resistance does not establish sinus origin. The abnormal discrete P-wave morphology supports a non-sinus atrial source in this recording.

Typical AVNRT established by resumption of one-to-one conduction: AVNRT can rarely continue with block below its circuit, so absent ventricular responses alone do not settle every case. Here the independently continuing discrete abnormal atrial rhythm favors AT, and resumption of conduction is not proof of nodal reentry.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: A patient has repeated narrow-complex tachycardia at 140–160/min. Each episode has one consistent P-wave morphology different from sinus rhythm, with an isoelectric interval between P waves. The atrial rate gradually accelerates at onset, and occasional AV block occurs without changing atrial timing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Focal atrial tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Focal Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: Focal atrial tachycardia

Recognize an Organized Non-Sinus Atrial Rhythm

**Focal AT produces atrial activation spreading from a localized source.** Discrete P waves differing from sinus morphology, often with intervening isoelectric segments, support the diagnosis.

Automatic activity can show warm-up and cool-down. Triggered activity and localized reentry are other mechanisms, so a focal ECG appearance does not prove that every such tachycardia is automatic.

The ventricular response depends on AV conduction and may be slower or irregular despite an organized atrial rhythm. Continuing atrial activity during AV block helps separate the atrial driver from an ordinary AVRT circuit.

Assess Burden and Select Treatment

**Incessant or frequently recurrent AT can cause tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy.** Assess symptoms, duration, ventricular function and reversible triggers instead of judging severity from one rate measurement.

Acute treatment depends on stability and mechanism. Adenosine can terminate some focal ATs or expose atrial activity without termination. Beta blockade or verapamil/diltiazem may help selected stable patients, with attention to hypotension, ventricular function and contraindications.

Catheter ablation is an important definitive option for recurrent symptomatic focal AT, particularly incessant AT associated with ventricular dysfunction. Mapping identifies the source; P-wave morphology offers clues but cannot replace invasive localization when ablation is performed. Atrial scarring can complicate the ECG distinction from macroreentry, and an isoelectric interval is not absolute proof against flutter. Reassess ventricular function after rhythm control when tachycardia-mediated dysfunction is suspected; improvement supports the causal contribution but does not exclude additional myocardial disease.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia: MAT has changing P-wave morphologies and irregular atrial timing. A single reproducible non-sinus morphology with an organized atrial cycle instead supports a single dominant atrial activation source.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: Typical AVNRT usually has abrupt onset and near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation. Persistent independent abnormal atrial activity and warm-up favor an atrial source rather than that usual nodal circuit.

Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT needs AV conduction as part of its circuit. Continued atrial tachycardia through AV block, together with non-sinus P waves and gradual acceleration, supports a focal atrial mechanism.

questions.question: During an exacerbation of COPD, a patient has an irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 125/min. A single lead shows at least three distinct P-wave morphologies, variable P–P and PR intervals, and isoelectric segments between atrial deflections. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial flutter with variable AV conduction
Sinus tachycardia with frequent atrial premature beats
questions.explanation:
Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: Multifocal atrial tachycardia

Use Atrial Morphology to Explain the Irregularity

**MAT is a rapid irregular atrial rhythm with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies in the same lead.** The conventional rate distinction from wandering atrial pacemaker is ==greater than 100/min==.

P–P, PR and R–R intervals can vary, while recognizable atrial depolarizations remain separated by isoelectric segments. Confirm that artefact or superimposed T waves are not being counted as extra morphologies.

Pulmonary disease, hypoxemia, pulmonary hypertension, electrolyte disturbances and theophylline exposure are relevant associations. The clinical setting supports the diagnosis but does not replace the ECG criteria.

Treat the Underlying Illness First

**Correct the precipitating respiratory or systemic disorder and potassium or magnesium abnormalities.** Review potentially contributory drugs while maintaining adequate treatment of the underlying pulmonary disease.

IV magnesium can be useful even when the measured level is normal. If symptomatic rapid conduction persists, selected beta blockers or verapamil/diltiazem can slow the ventricular response; choose according to bronchospasm, pressure, LV function and other contraindications.

Electrical cardioversion and conventional rhythm drugs generally do not provide durable control of this multifocal atrial process. MAT alone does not establish the AF-related indication for anticoagulation; look for any separate indication rather than treating every irregular pulse as AF. Follow clinical recovery and repeat the ECG when needed. Persistent drug-refractory tachycardia with associated ventricular dysfunction warrants specialist assessment, while an acute pulmonary trigger should not lead directly to invasive treatment without an attempt to correct that driver.

Rhythm | Atrial finding | Timing clue

MAT | At least 3 discrete P morphologies in one lead | Irregular P–P; rate >100/min

Wandering atrial pacemaker | Multiple discrete P morphologies | Similar pattern at a slower rate

AF | No consistent discrete P sequence | Irregular ventricular response unless another mechanism intervenes

Flutter with variable block | Repeating organized atrial activation | Irregular ventricular conduction with organized atrial cycle

Atrial fibrillation: AF has disorganized atrial activation without consistently identifiable discrete P waves. Irregularity alone is insufficient: the multiple discrete P morphologies and intervening isoelectric baseline support MAT.

Atrial flutter with variable AV conduction: Variable conduction can make flutter ventricular intervals irregular, but the underlying atrial cycle is usually organized and repetitive. Changing P-wave morphologies and irregular atrial intervals favor MAT.

Sinus tachycardia with frequent atrial premature beats: Sinus rhythm with ectopy retains a dominant sinus sequence interrupted by premature beats. A sustained irregular atrial rhythm with several recurring morphologies and no dominant sinus cycle is more consistent with MAT.

questions.question: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia runs at 150/min. During a monitored diagnostic maneuver, ventricular conduction briefly slows and continuous atrial activity at 300/min becomes visible, with repetitive negative deflections in the inferior leads. Which diagnosis best explains the original rhythm?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia with one-to-one conduction
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Atrial flutter with two-to-one AV conduction
questions.explanation:
Atrial Flutter With Concealed Two-to-One Conduction

Correct answer: Atrial flutter with two-to-one AV conduction

Find the Hidden Atrial Cycle

**Flutter with 2:1 conduction can masquerade as a regular SVT because alternate atrial deflections are concealed by QRS or T waves.** A ventricular rate near 150/min is a useful prompt to inspect the atria, not a diagnostic criterion by itself.

The usual atrial rate is approximately 250–330/min, but medications, scarring and other substrates can change it. Determine the actual atrial rate rather than assuming that every flutter cycle is exactly 200 ms.

Counterclockwise typical flutter often produces negative inferior flutter waves and positive activity in V1. Surface morphology suggests but does not definitively establish cavotricuspid-isthmus dependence.

Diagnostic Slowing Does Not Necessarily Terminate Flutter

**Transient AV nodal block may reveal the atrial rhythm while the macroreentrant circuit continues.** Record the full tracing to distinguish ventricular slowing from conversion to sinus rhythm.

Adenosine is not routine curative treatment for flutter. When used diagnostically in uncertainty, it requires monitoring and rescue readiness because AF induction or rebound rapid conduction can occur.

After recognition, assess stability, ventricular function, episode duration and thromboembolic protection before choosing rate control, cardioversion or ablation. Flutter may be difficult to rate-control, and typical flutter often responds well to CTI ablation. A successful flutter intervention does not eliminate later AF or automatically end anticoagulation requirements. The immediate diagnostic lesson is to count atrial events during slowed conduction; rate labels alone can miss the rhythm that determines subsequent treatment.

Focal atrial tachycardia with one-to-one conduction: Focal AT can continue through AV block, but one-to-one conduction would not explain the original atrial-to-ventricular ratio of two. Continuous repetitive flutter activity further favors macroreentry over a discrete focal P-wave pattern.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: AVNRT can obscure atrial activity near the QRS, but the newly visible atrial cycle is twice the original ventricular rate and continues independently as conduction slows. This supports an atrial driver rather than ordinary one-to-one nodal reentry.

Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT requires atria and ventricles in its circuit. A continuing atrial rhythm at 300/min while the ventricular response slows is inconsistent with the usual one-to-one accessory-pathway circuit.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: After cardiac surgery, an adult has narrow-complex tachycardia that gradually accelerates to 135/min and later slows gradually. Sinus P waves at 85/min march independently through the rhythm, and the QRS morphology matches normally conducted baseline beats. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia with variable AV block
Orthodromic AV reentry through an accessory pathway
Typical slow–fast AV nodal reentry
Enhanced automaticity producing focal junctional tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Nonreentrant Junctional Tachycardia

Correct answer: Enhanced automaticity producing focal junctional tachycardia

Recognize a Junctional Driver

**Focal junctional tachycardia arises from abnormal impulse formation near the AV node or proximal His region.** A narrow QRS rhythm with AV dissociation can occur because the junctional rate exceeds the sinus rate.

Warm-up and cool-down favor an automatic mechanism over abrupt reentry. Some cases have retrograde atrial conduction, even one-to-one, which can make the surface rhythm resemble AVNRT or AVRT.

AV dissociation rules out ordinary AVRT but does not absolutely exclude every AVNRT variant. A careful mechanism assessment is therefore more reliable than using a single surface sign as universal proof.

Address the Context and Hemodynamic Consequences

**Assess postoperative stress, catecholamine exposure, ischemia, electrolyte disturbance and medication toxicity.** The setting and ventricular function influence both urgency and treatment.

Treat reversible drivers and obtain specialist rhythm input. Selected beta blockers or other antiarrhythmics can be used according to the clinical substrate; evidence in adults is limited, and a pediatric postoperative regimen should not be transferred automatically.

Adenosine may reveal atrial nonparticipation but does not reliably terminate automatic junctional tachycardia. Electrical cardioversion is also less likely to provide durable suppression of an automatic focus than of a reentrant circuit. Persistent symptomatic or hemodynamically important disease can require specialized treatment, including selected ablation with attention to AV-block risk. Avoid reflexly selecting slow-pathway ablation merely because the rhythm arises near the AV junction; the target and procedural risks depend on the demonstrated mechanism.

Focal atrial tachycardia with variable AV block: Focal AT requires the rapid driver to be atrial. Here the atrial rate is slower than the ventricular rhythm and independent of it, so the atria are not supplying the tachycardic impulse sequence.

Orthodromic AV reentry through an accessory pathway: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT needs the atria and ventricles as circuit components. Sustained tachycardia with independent slower atrial activity argues against that mechanism rather than an accessory-pathway return limb.

Typical slow–fast AV nodal reentry: AVNRT is a reentrant mechanism, usually with abrupt onset and offset. Although rare AVNRT variants can dissociate the atria, gradual rate behavior and the postoperative context favor automatic junctional tachycardia here.

questions.question: An electrophysiology study demonstrates a regular reentrant tachycardia using antegrade conduction through the AV node and His–Purkinje system, with retrograde return through an atrioventricular accessory pathway. Which classification is correct?
options: Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Atrial tachycardia with bystander pre-excitation
questions.explanation:
Orthodromic and Antidromic AV Reentry

Correct answer: Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia

Name the Circuit by Antegrade Activation

**Orthodromic AVRT conducts from atrium to ventricle through the AV node and His–Purkinje system, then returns through an accessory pathway.** Ventricular activation is usually narrow because the normal conduction system activates it.

Antidromic AVRT activates the ventricle antegradely through an accessory pathway and returns through the AV node or another accessory pathway. Its QRS is pre-excited and wide.

QRS width supports the mechanism but is not sufficient alone: orthodromic AVRT can develop bundle-branch aberrancy, while wide-complex tachycardia has several other causes.

Distinguish Pathway Participation From Pathway Presence

**A manifest accessory pathway can coexist with a rhythm that does not use it as a necessary circuit limb.** AF, flutter, focal AT or AVNRT can conduct through a bystander pathway.

Electrophysiological maneuvers establish whether pathway conduction is required for the tachycardia. That distinction determines the mechanism and helps select the ablation target.

Acute treatment depends on stability, regularity, QRS pattern and whether pre-excited AF is possible. A nodal-blocking approach suitable for ordinary regular orthodromic AVRT must not be transferred to irregular pre-excited AF. For recurrent symptomatic AVRT, accessory-pathway ablation is a definitive option after discussion of pathway location, procedural risk and patient preferences. A clear circuit description is more informative than using the presence of a delta wave as a general label for every episode of palpitations.

Mechanism | Antegrade limb | Retrograde limb | Usual QRS

Orthodromic AVRT | AV node–His–Purkinje | Accessory pathway | Narrow unless aberrancy

Antidromic AVRT | Accessory pathway | AV node or another pathway | Wide and pre-excited

Typical AVNRT | Slow nodal pathway | Fast nodal pathway | Usually narrow

Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Antidromic AVRT uses an accessory pathway for antegrade ventricular activation, producing a pre-excited QRS. The antegrade limb here is the normal AV nodal and His–Purkinje route.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: Typical AVNRT uses functionally distinct nodal pathways rather than requiring an atrioventricular accessory pathway and the ventricle in the circuit. The demonstrated extranodal retrograde limb establishes AVRT.

Orthodromic and Antidromic AV Reentry

Correct answer: B — Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia

Name the Circuit by Antegrade Activation

  • Orthodromic AVRT conducts from atrium to ventricle through the AV node and His–Purkinje system, then returns through an accessory pathway. Ventricular activation is usually narrow because the normal conduction system activates it.
    • Antidromic AVRT activates the ventricle antegradely through an accessory pathway and returns through the AV node or another accessory pathway. Its QRS is pre-excited and wide.
    • QRS width supports the mechanism but is not sufficient alone: orthodromic AVRT can develop bundle-branch aberrancy, while wide-complex tachycardia has several other causes.

Distinguish Pathway Participation From Pathway Presence

  • A manifest accessory pathway can coexist with a rhythm that does not use it as a necessary circuit limb. AF, flutter, focal AT or AVNRT can conduct through a bystander pathway.
    • Electrophysiological maneuvers establish whether pathway conduction is required for the tachycardia. That distinction determines the mechanism and helps select the ablation target.

For recurrent symptomatic AVRT, accessory-pathway ablation is a definitive option after discussion of pathway location, procedural risk and patient preferences. A clear circuit description is more informative than using the presence of a delta wave as a general label for every episode of palpitations.

questions.explanation:
Concealed Accessory Pathways

Correct answer: The pathway can sustain orthodromic AVRT without producing resting ventricular pre-excitation

Concealed Refers to the Direction of Conduction

**A concealed accessory pathway conducts retrogradely and therefore does not produce a delta wave in sinus rhythm.** It can nevertheless participate as the return limb of orthodromic AVRT.

During tachycardia, the AV node and His–Purkinje system activate the ventricle antegradely, and the pathway returns activation to the atrium. The usual narrow QRS does not imply absence of an accessory connection.

Distinguish a proven retrograde-only pathway from intermittent manifest pre-excitation. A normal single ECG in the latter setting may reflect changing competition or pathway conduction rather than permanent absence of antegrade capability.

Connect Direction to Risk and Treatment

**The pre-excited AF mechanism of very rapid antegrade pathway conduction does not arise through a genuinely retrograde-only pathway.** This does not mean that every palpitation is benign or that other cardiac risks have been excluded.

Recurrent symptomatic orthodromic AVRT can warrant ablation despite a normal baseline ECG. Mapping establishes location and participation; septal proximity to the normal conduction system affects the procedural discussion.

Selected AV nodal drugs may be appropriate for ordinary orthodromic AVRT when ablation is not chosen, taking account of pressure, ventricular function and contraindications. Do not use the absence of a resting delta wave as the sole reason to give nodal blockade during an undiagnosed irregular wide-complex episode. The direction demonstrated on EPS provides stronger evidence than an isolated surface tracing. Preserve the mechanism in the clinical record so later care distinguishes concealed reentry from manifest pre-excitation and its different emergency implications.

The pathway creates the same rapid pre-excited AF mechanism as a short-refractory antegrade pathway: Rapid ventricular pre-excitation during AF requires antegrade accessory conduction. A truly retrograde-only pathway does not supply that mechanism, although AF and other independent risks may still occur.

Absence of a delta wave makes the demonstrated pathway incapable of sustaining AVRT: A delta wave requires antegrade pathway conduction. Retrograde conduction can close an orthodromic reentry circuit even when antegrade conduction and resting ventricular activation are normal.

The pathway can provide the antegrade limb of antidromic AVRT: The demonstrated pathway has no antegrade conduction. It can return activation to the atrium but cannot itself provide the antegrade pre-excited limb required for antidromic AVRT.

questions.explanation:
Recognition of Pre-Excited Atrial Fibrillation

Correct answer: Atrial fibrillation with antegrade accessory-pathway conduction

Variable Ventricular Activation Signals a Different Emergency

**Pre-excited AF can deliver rapid irregular atrial impulses to the ventricle through an accessory pathway.** Changing competition between AV nodal and accessory conduction produces varying QRS width and morphology.

A prior short PR and delta wave establish manifest pre-excitation as a relevant substrate. The acute tracing must still be interpreted directly; not every wide rhythm in a patient with an accessory pathway is AVRT.

A pathway with a short antegrade refractory period can permit dangerously rapid ventricular responses and degeneration to VF. Assess pulse and perfusion continuously rather than waiting for a particular displayed average rate.

Avoid the Ordinary AF Rate-Control Reflex

**AV nodal blocking drugs are contraindicated in pre-excited AF because ventricular acceleration and VF can occur.** The US 2023 guideline includes adenosine, beta blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin and amiodarone in this warning.

Unstable patients require immediate electrical cardioversion. In suitable stable patients, IV procainamide or ibutilide can be used with monitoring as alternatives to electrical conversion.

If polymorphic VT or VF is present, follow the appropriate unsynchronized-defibrillation pathway; an uncertain rapidly deteriorating wide-complex rhythm must not be exposed to empirical nodal blockade. After stabilization, refer for accessory-pathway assessment and ablation. The crucial distinction is between regular AV-node-dependent reentry, where nodal interruption can terminate the circuit, and irregular antegrade pathway conduction during AF, where that same drug strategy can be hazardous.

Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Antidromic AVRT produces pre-excited wide complexes, but its reentrant cycle is ordinarily regular. The very irregular intervals and changing degrees of pre-excitation favor AF conducting through both available routes.

AF with fixed bundle-branch aberrancy: AF with bundle-branch disease can be irregular and wide, but fixed aberrancy generally preserves a more consistent conduction pattern. Known manifest pre-excitation and extreme variable ventricular activation raise concern for accessory conduction.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia: Polymorphic VT is an important dangerous wide-complex alternative. Here the prior delta wave and irregularly variable pre-excited pattern specifically support AF with accessory conduction, although diagnostic uncertainty must still be managed safely.

AHA adult advanced life support guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001376

questions.question: During EPS for manifest pre-excitation, induced AF has a shortest pre-excited R–R interval of 220 ms. Which interpretation best matches ESC 2019 risk stratification?
options: The measurement primarily establishes slow retrograde pathway conduction
The measurement is reassuring because the average ventricular rate is lower
Risk cannot be assessed until a spontaneous clinical AF episode is recorded
The pathway has a high-risk antegrade conduction property supporting ablation discussion
questions.explanation:
High-Risk Accessory-Pathway Conduction

Correct answer: The pathway has a high-risk antegrade conduction property supporting ablation discussion

Use the Correct Interval and Threshold

**SPERRI is the shortest pre-excited R–R interval during AF.** ESC 2019 identifies ==SPERRI ≤250 ms== as a high-risk accessory-pathway feature; 220 ms clearly meets that criterion.

Measure genuinely pre-excited complexes and distinguish artefact, fusion and non-pre-excited conduction. A short interval shows that the pathway can deliver closely spaced impulses to the ventricular myocardium.

The pathway effective refractory period is a separate measurement; ==antegrade AP ERP ≤250 ms== is another high-risk feature. The two tests address related conduction properties but are not interchangeable labels.

Integrate the Electrophysiological Findings

**Multiple pathways and inducible accessory-pathway-mediated tachycardia also contribute to the ESC high-risk framework.** Catecholamine challenge can expose conduction properties not apparent under baseline conditions.

High-risk findings support catheter ablation after discussion of benefits and procedural risk, including AV-block risk near the septal conduction system. A favorable current symptom history does not erase a documented rapid pathway.

Conversely, a threshold predicts risk rather than guaranteeing VF in an individual. Explain uncertainty without describing observation as equivalent protection against an established high-risk substrate. Assess occupation, athletics, prior syncope and structural disease as part of the overall decision. Do not confuse a retrograde-only concealed pathway with a manifest pathway capable of rapid antegrade AF conduction. After successful ablation, verify pathway elimination and arrange follow-up appropriate to symptoms and procedural findings.

EPS finding | ESC 2019 high-risk feature

Shortest pre-excited RR during AF | ≤250 ms

Antegrade accessory-pathway ERP | ≤250 ms

Pathway number | Multiple accessory pathways

Inducibility | Accessory-pathway-mediated tachycardia at baseline or catecholamine challenge

The measurement primarily establishes slow retrograde pathway conduction: The pre-excited R–R interval during AF reflects antegrade delivery to the ventricle. Slowly conducting retrograde pathways are relevant to PJRT but do not explain this rapid antegrade property.

The measurement is reassuring because the average ventricular rate is lower: SPERRI measures the fastest demonstrated pre-excited ventricular conduction rather than the average rate. Longer intervening intervals do not neutralize a documented very short pre-excited interval.

Risk cannot be assessed until a spontaneous clinical AF episode is recorded: Induced AF during a properly conducted EPS can assess pathway conduction. A spontaneous dangerous episode is not required before acting on a qualifying high-risk electrophysiological finding.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: Months after left atrial AF ablation, a patient develops sustained organized atrial tachycardia. The surface waves differ from classic inferior saw-tooth flutter. Prior CTI block remains intact. Which approach best defines the substrate before repeat ablation?
options: Create a mitral isthmus line solely from the history of left atrial ablation
Repeat the CTI line solely because the rhythm is called flutter
Select a focal ablation target solely because an isoelectric interval is visible
Activation and entrainment assessment to identify the actual atrial circuit and critical conduction channel
questions.explanation:
Atypical Scar-Related Atrial Flutter

Correct answer: Activation and entrainment assessment to identify the actual atrial circuit and critical conduction channel

Atypical Flutter Describes a Different Circuit Family

**Non-CTI-dependent macroreentrant AT can use anatomical barriers, surgical scars or prior ablation lesions.** Left atrial examples include perimitral and roof-dependent circuits.

Prior ablation can create slow-conduction channels or incomplete lines that permit organized reentry. The arrhythmia may appear after a period of sinus rhythm and need not resemble the original AF.

Surface morphology is less reliable after atrial scarring. Atypical wave appearance does not exclude a right atrial circuit, and a visually discrete P wave does not prove a nonreentrant focal mechanism.

Map Before Adding Lesions

**Activation mapping and appropriate entrainment maneuvers identify circuit participation and a critical isthmus.** Integrate local signals with the full tachycardia cycle rather than ablating the earliest visible deflection without context.

Treat a mapped channel or complete an indicated line, then verify its intended conduction endpoint. Termination alone can be misleading if a gap remains or the rhythm changes to another circuit.

Assess symptoms, ventricular response, LV function and anticoagulation before intervention. Cardioversion is available for acute compromise or selected symptom relief, but recurrent scar-related tachycardia often requires a mechanism-based durable plan. Discuss that repeat atrial procedures can be more complex than a first CTI ablation and can uncover multiple circuits. Avoid applying a single ECG label as a procedural map; the anatomy and electrophysiology determine which lesion is useful.

Create a mitral isthmus line solely from the history of left atrial ablation: Perimitral reentry is plausible, but roof-dependent or other scar-related circuits can also occur. An empirical line without circuit definition may fail to address the rhythm and add further proarrhythmic gaps.

Repeat the CTI line solely because the rhythm is called flutter: A CTI line treats a demonstrated isthmus-dependent circuit. Intact block and a post-left-atrial-ablation substrate raise other possibilities; the generic flutter label does not establish a CTI gap.

Select a focal ablation target solely because an isoelectric interval is visible: A discrete-looking surface pattern can occur with scar-related macroreentry. An isoelectric interval does not prove focal origin when atrial activation is altered by prior lesions.

questions.question: A smartwatch using photoplethysmography repeatedly reports an irregular pulse in an asymptomatic adult. No ECG tracing has been recorded. Which next step is most appropriate before establishing a clinical AF diagnosis?
options: Use the absence of palpitations to dismiss the alerts
Diagnose AF from repeated optical alerts because repetition removes false positives
Obtain an interpretable ECG recording and have the rhythm reviewed by a qualified clinician
Use left atrial enlargement on echocardiography as confirmation
questions.explanation:
ECG Confirmation of Suspected Atrial Fibrillation

Correct answer: Obtain an interpretable ECG recording and have the rhythm reviewed by a qualified clinician

An Optical Pulse Signal Is a Screening Clue

**Clinical AF requires ECG documentation rather than photoplethysmographic irregularity alone.** A wearable that records an actual ECG is different from one that supplies only an optical pulse alert.

Review for irregular ventricular intervals and absence of a consistent repeating P-wave sequence, recognizing that pacing or AV conduction disease can alter the ventricular pattern. A clinician should inspect the tracing rather than accept an automated label uncritically.

Choose a 12-lead ECG if the rhythm is present, or an appropriate ambulatory or patient-recorded ECG strategy when episodes are intermittent. A normal symptom-free snapshot does not exclude paroxysmal AF.

Interpret Recording Duration in Context

**ESC 2024 recognizes AF across a conventional 12-lead recording and interpretable single- or multilead ECG devices.** A conventional 12-lead ECG is usually ten seconds; it need not be extended to thirty seconds to count as that recording.

Thirty seconds or longer has generally been the consensus convention for ambulatory single- or multilead episodes, but the evidence for a universal minimum is limited and the clinical context matters. Do not turn an arbitrary duration into proof of treatment benefit.

Brief device-detected atrial episodes require confirmation and an assessment distinct from automatically treating every alert as established clinical AF. Once AF is confirmed, evaluate comorbidity, stroke risk and rate or rhythm needs independently of symptoms. If the tracing instead shows ectopy, flutter or artefact, address that actual finding. This sequence avoids both missing silent AF and exposing a patient to diagnosis-specific treatment without a verified rhythm.

Use the absence of palpitations to dismiss the alerts: AF can be asymptomatic, so symptom absence cannot exclude it. The appropriate response is proportionate confirmatory recording rather than either immediate labelling or dismissal.

Diagnose AF from repeated optical alerts because repetition removes false positives: Repeated alerts increase the reason to investigate but do not convert pulse sensing into atrial electrical documentation. Ectopy and artefact can generate recurrent optical irregularity.

Use left atrial enlargement on echocardiography as confirmation: Atrial enlargement can identify substrate and influence management, but it is not rhythm documentation. Echo cannot establish that an optical alert represented AF rather than another irregular rhythm.

questions.question: During a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 165/min, atrial deflections continue independently at 78/min. An occasional narrow complex matching the baseline sinus QRS appears within the tachycardia. Which mechanism is most strongly supported?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia conducted with fixed bundle-branch block
Orthodromic AVRT with bundle-branch aberrancy
Ventricular tachycardia with intermittent sinus capture
Antidromic AVRT with variable pre-excitation
questions.explanation:
AV Dissociation and Capture During Wide-Complex Tachycardia

Correct answer: Ventricular tachycardia with intermittent sinus capture

Look for Independent Atrial and Ventricular Activation

**AV dissociation during a wide-complex tachycardia strongly supports VT.** Atrial depolarizations march through at a different rate without a consistent relationship to the ventricular complexes.

A capture beat occurs when a supraventricular impulse reaches the ventricle when conduction and myocardial refractoriness permit, producing a relatively normal complex within the ventricular rhythm. A fusion beat combines supraventricular and ventricular activation and has an intermediate morphology.

Confirm that a narrow deflection is a genuine capture complex rather than artefact or a change in aberrancy. Compare with baseline QRS morphology and inspect atrial timing across multiple leads.

Use Positive Signs Without Overinterpreting Their Absence

**Absence of visible dissociation, capture or fusion does not exclude VT.** Retrograde ventriculoatrial conduction can produce an apparent one-to-one association, and atrial activity may be buried in the QRS or T wave.

Integrate prior MI or cardiomyopathy, baseline ECG, QRS morphology and the overall clinical setting. Surface algorithms can support diagnosis but do not justify assuming SVT whenever one criterion is absent.

Rare AV nodal or junctional mechanisms can exhibit atrial dissociation, so interpret the entire tracing and seek expert electrophysiological assessment when needed. The combination here, including a sinus-capture complex, is particularly supportive of VT. Maintain a treatment strategy compatible with VT while uncertainty remains: empirical verapamil in an undifferentiated wide rhythm can cause collapse. Hemodynamic stability permits assessment but does not establish supraventricular origin. If attributable instability develops, prioritize electrical treatment rather than waiting for every diagnostic sign to appear.

Focal atrial tachycardia conducted with fixed bundle-branch block: An atrial driver would need to account for the faster ventricular activation. The observed atrial rate is slower and independent, while a sinus impulse occasionally captures the ventricle.

Orthodromic AVRT with bundle-branch aberrancy: AVRT requires coordinated atrial and ventricular participation in its reentrant loop. Independent slower atrial activity and an intervening sinus-capture complex oppose that ordinary circuit.

Antidromic AVRT with variable pre-excitation: Antidromic AVRT produces wide ventricular activation through an accessory pathway, but ordinary AVRT requires atrial participation. Slower dissociated atrial activity and sinus capture instead support an independent ventricular rhythm.

questions.question: A patient with previous MI has regular wide-complex tachycardia. No RS complex is present in any precordial lead. Atrial activity cannot be confidently identified. Which interpretation is best?
options: The tracing favors SVT because an RS-interval measurement is unavailable
The tracing favors SVT because atrial dissociation has not been demonstrated
The morphology supports VT; lack of visible AV dissociation does not negate that evidence
The absence of RS complexes establishes antidromic AVRT through an accessory pathway
questions.explanation:
Morphological Criteria in Regular Wide-Complex Tachycardia

Correct answer: The morphology supports VT; lack of visible AV dissociation does not negate that evidence

Apply the Sequence to the Actual Tracing

**Absence of an RS complex in every precordial lead is a VT criterion in the Brugada algorithm for regular wide-complex tachycardia.** If an RS complex is present, a longest precordial RS interval greater than 100 ms is another supporting criterion.

The sequence then considers AV dissociation and morphology in selected precordial leads. A negative earlier step means proceed through the assessment; it does not establish SVT by itself.

Concordance means that precordial complexes share the same predominant polarity. Review the complete complexes rather than equating any prominent R wave with concordance.

Recognize the Limits of Surface Algorithms

**ECG algorithms provide probabilistic evidence and must be interpreted with substrate and baseline conduction.** Pre-excitation, antiarrhythmic effects, electrolyte disturbance and unusual ventricular exit sites can complicate interpretation.

A prior infarction increases concern for scar-related VT. Compare the tachycardia with a previous sinus tracing, and seek capture, fusion or atrial dissociation without requiring them all to be visible.

Vereckei approaches use additional features such as initial aVR activation and relative initial versus terminal ventricular activation velocity; they are alternative structured assessments rather than a guarantee of perfect discrimination. An initial R in aVR can support ventricular origin, but no isolated sign should substitute for inspection of the full rhythm. Manage uncertain wide-complex tachycardia with a VT-compatible strategy and rescue readiness. Do not use preserved blood pressure or absent visible atrial dissociation to justify empirical verapamil. Document a twelve-lead ECG when feasible, but deterioration requires prompt electrical treatment rather than completion of a diagnostic checklist.

The tracing favors SVT because an RS-interval measurement is unavailable: In the Brugada sequence, absence of RS complexes in all precordial leads itself supports VT. Measuring an RS interval is the next step when an RS complex exists, not a prerequisite for using the first criterion.

The tracing favors SVT because atrial dissociation has not been demonstrated: Visible dissociation strongly supports VT, but many VTs have concealed atrial activity or retrograde conduction. Its absence is not a positive criterion establishing supraventricular origin.

The absence of RS complexes establishes antidromic AVRT through an accessory pathway: Pre-excited tachycardia can mimic ventricular-origin morphology, so this remains a differential. Absence of precordial RS complexes does not establish accessory-pathway participation, particularly in a patient with an infarct substrate.

ESC ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

ESC SVT guideline: wide-complex differential, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: Two monitored patients develop polymorphic VT. Between episodes, patient X has QTc 560 ms after a QT-prolonging drug and a pause preceding onset; patient Y has QTc 420 ms with acute ischemic chest pain. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Both most likely have CPVT because each has a polymorphic rhythm
Both have torsades because beat-to-beat QRS morphology varies
X most likely has ischemic polymorphic VT, while Y has drug-induced torsades
X has a torsades phenotype; Y requires assessment for ischemia-associated polymorphic VT rather than automatic torsades labelling
questions.explanation:
Torsades Versus Polymorphic VT With a Normal QT

Correct answer: X has a torsades phenotype; Y requires assessment for ischemia-associated polymorphic VT rather than automatic torsades labelling

Measure Repolarization Outside the Ventricular Run

**Torsades de pointes is polymorphic VT associated with prolonged QT in the intervening rhythm.** The apparent twisting pattern alone is insufficient to identify its mechanism.

Review a reliable baseline or interepisode ECG, the rate, drugs and electrolytes. QT interpretation is difficult during a rapid ventricular run, and broad QRS complexes or unusual T–U morphology can complicate automated measurements.

A short–long–short sequence or pause-dependent onset supports acquired long-QT torsades. Assess bradycardia, potassium and magnesium depletion, drug interactions and impaired drug clearance.

The Distinction Changes Recurrence Treatment

**Sustained polymorphic VT requires an immediate unsynchronized shock because reliable synchronization is difficult.** Loss of pulse requires the shockable-arrest pathway; an apparently tolerable brief run still warrants urgent monitoring and cause assessment.

For recurrent long-QT torsades, magnesium and correction of the cause are important; remove QT-prolonging agents and correct electrolyte deficiency. Selected recurrent acquired pause-dependent cases may require rate acceleration through pacing or isoproterenol under specialist monitoring.

With a normal QT, investigate ischemia and other substrates; urgent coronary assessment and appropriate antiarrhythmic therapy can be consequential. AHA 2025 does not recommend routine magnesium simply for normal-QT polymorphic VT. Magnesium remains appropriate for documented deficiency, which is a separate indication. Do not extrapolate isoproterenol used in acquired bradycardia-related torsades to congenital long-QT disease or active ischemia without reviewing the mechanism. A treatment that is helpful in one polymorphic-rhythm phenotype can be ineffective or harmful in another.

Both most likely have CPVT because each has a polymorphic rhythm: CPVT is considered with adrenergically provoked bidirectional or polymorphic VT, typically with a normal resting ECG and no explanatory structural disease. Neither polymorphism alone nor these two supplied triggers establishes that inherited syndrome.

Both have torsades because beat-to-beat QRS morphology varies: Polymorphic morphology describes ventricular activation, but torsades specifically occurs in the setting of prolonged repolarization. Normal-QT polymorphic VT has a different etiological and treatment assessment.

X most likely has ischemic polymorphic VT, while Y has drug-induced torsades: The supplied interepisode QT and pause-dependent onset support acquired long-QT torsades in X. Acute ischemic symptoms with a normal QT support a different mechanism in Y rather than the reversed assignment.

questions.question: An older patient taking digoxin develops vomiting, new renal impairment and ventricular tachycardia with alternating frontal QRS axis on successive beats. The resting QT before the episode was not prolonged. Which cause is most likely?
options: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Digoxin toxicity
Acquired long-QT torsades de pointes
Scar-related monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Bidirectional Ventricular Tachycardia in Clinical Context

Correct answer: Digoxin toxicity

A Pattern Can Have More Than One Cause

**Bidirectional VT shows beat-to-beat alternation of the frontal QRS axis.** Important associations include digoxin toxicity, CPVT, Andersen–Tawil syndrome and occasionally acute myocardial disease.

Digoxin-related sodium–potassium ATPase inhibition can cause intracellular calcium overload and triggered activity. Renal impairment reduces clearance and makes a previously tolerated chronic regimen hazardous.

Ask about dosing changes, interacting medicines and gastrointestinal or neurological symptoms. A new drug interaction can raise exposure without a newly increased digoxin prescription.

Treat the Toxic Syndrome Rather Than the ECG Label Alone

**Stop digoxin and assess rhythm, perfusion, renal function and electrolytes urgently.** Life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia in suspected digoxin toxicity warrants digoxin immune Fab and specialist toxicology/cardiology support.

Measure a properly timed concentration, generally at least six hours after a dose, but do not postpone antidotal treatment of life-threatening toxicity to await a level. Clinical toxicity can occur at concentrations that appear acceptable in a vulnerable patient.

Potassium abnormalities require careful interpretation: depletion can increase susceptibility, while substantial toxicity can produce hyperkalemia. Monitor potassium closely after Fab because it may fall as the pharmacological effect reverses. Routine total digoxin assays become difficult to interpret after Fab because bound drug contributes to the measured result. Correct the precipitating renal or interaction problem and reassess the need for future treatment. A younger patient with exertional syncope and an otherwise normal evaluation would instead need assessment for CPVT; the same morphology does not establish the same cause in every clinical setting.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia: CPVT can produce bidirectional VT, usually during adrenergic stress in a patient without explanatory structural disease. New renal impairment, digoxin exposure and gastrointestinal symptoms make an acquired toxic mechanism more likely here.

Acquired long-QT torsades de pointes: Drug-induced torsades is associated with prolonged repolarization and commonly pause-dependent polymorphic VT. Alternation between two ventricular axes with a previously normal QT and this exposure history favors digoxin toxicity.

Scar-related monomorphic ventricular tachycardia: Scar reentry is important in structural heart disease and generally produces a stable monomorphic pattern during a given episode. Beat-to-beat axis alternation and systemic digoxin-toxicity clues require a different explanation.

questions.question: Years after MI, a patient has recurrent sustained monomorphic VT. Induced clinical VT causes hypotension too rapidly for prolonged activation mapping. Which approach best explains a useful ablation strategy?
options: Target the earliest isolated PVC as the presumed source of the sustained scar VT
Restrict mapping to prolonged activation and entrainment during the hypotensive clinical VT
Map abnormal scar channels and electrograms during a tolerated rhythm to target the reentry substrate
Use a single pace-map match as proof of the entire critical reentry isthmus
questions.explanation:
Scar Reentry and Substrate Mapping

Correct answer: Map abnormal scar channels and electrograms during a tolerated rhythm to target the reentry substrate

Surviving Myocardium Within Fibrosis Supports Reentry

**Postinfarction monomorphic VT commonly uses slow conduction through surviving myocardial bundles within or along scar.** Fixed and functional block permit a reentrant circuit rather than a simple uniformly dead region.

Different exits from related channels can produce different VT morphologies. A stable QRS pattern during one episode does not prove that only one possible circuit exists in the ventricle.

The substrate can be endocardial, intramural or epicardial. Nonischemic cardiomyopathy can have a different distribution, so surface or endocardial findings do not map every disease identically.

Choose Mapping According to Hemodynamic Tolerance

**Activation and entrainment mapping can define circuit participation when VT is sufficiently tolerated.** When sustained mapping is unsafe, substrate assessment during sinus or paced rhythm can identify abnormal potentials and conduction channels.

Low voltage, delayed or fractionated signals and local abnormal ventricular activities help characterize potential targets. Integrate imaging, electroanatomic mapping and any available tachycardia evidence rather than treating every low-voltage point as an essential isthmus.

Pace mapping approximates the ventricular exit pattern and can complement other methods, but its spatial and mechanistic limitations prevent equating one excellent match with proof of the entire circuit. Ablation may target channels or a broader abnormal substrate according to the case; procedural endpoints include clinical VT noninducibility and appropriate substrate assessment. Acute noninducibility does not guarantee lifelong freedom from recurrence because additional circuits, inaccessible tissue or evolving disease can remain. Plan for hemodynamic deterioration and selected support when needed, and continue independent HF and ICD management. The inability to sustain VT for detailed activation mapping does not by itself make ablation impossible; it changes the mapping and procedural-risk strategy.

Target the earliest isolated PVC as the presumed source of the sustained scar VT: Activation mapping of a trigger PVC is valuable for selected focal arrhythmias or PVC-triggered VF. In established scar reentry, an incidental PVC need not identify the critical sustaining channel and cannot substitute for circuit or substrate assessment.

Restrict mapping to prolonged activation and entrainment during the hypotensive clinical VT: Activation and entrainment are useful when VT can be sustained safely. Repeated prolonged induction in this poorly tolerated rhythm can worsen perfusion; substrate mapping provides information during a more tolerable rhythm.

Use a single pace-map match as proof of the entire critical reentry isthmus: Pace mapping can identify an exit region or support localization. A matching surface QRS does not by itself prove participation of that site in the essential channel or define the full circuit.

HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS ventricular arrhythmia ablation consensus, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1002/joa3.12185

ESC ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

questions.question: A young adult has catecholamine-associated monomorphic VT with an LBBB-like pattern and inferior axis. Baseline ECG, echo and directed structural evaluation are reassuring. Adenosine terminates a monitored episode. Which interpretation is most likely?
options: Scar-mediated macroreentrant VT established by the broad QRS
Typical slow–fast AVNRT established by adenosine termination
Left posterior fascicular reentrant VT
Idiopathic outflow-tract VT, commonly related to cAMP-mediated triggered activity
questions.explanation:
Outflow-Tract Ventricular Tachycardia

Correct answer: Idiopathic outflow-tract VT, commonly related to cAMP-mediated triggered activity

Use Morphology as a Localization Clue

**RVOT arrhythmias commonly have an LBBB-like QRS and inferior axis.** Activation spreads away from a superior right ventricular source toward the inferior leads.

LV outflow and adjacent structures can produce overlapping appearances. Precordial transition and more detailed mapping help refine origin, but a single broad morphology should not be treated as an exact anatomical map.

An apparently idiopathic outflow rhythm still requires an appropriate structural and family assessment. ARVC and other substrates can mimic a right ventricular origin, especially when syncope, abnormal sinus ECG or multiple morphologies are present.

Connect Triggered Activity to the Drug Response

**Many idiopathic outflow VTs involve cAMP-dependent calcium loading and delayed afterdepolarization-mediated triggered activity.** Exercise or emotional stress can increase frequency, and adenosine can terminate selected episodes.

Adenosine termination therefore does not uniquely establish AVNRT or AVRT. In an uncertain wide-complex rhythm, its consideration is restricted to an appropriate stable, regular monomorphic phenotype with rescue readiness.

Treatment depends on symptoms, burden, ventricular function and preference. Beta blockers can be useful for an adrenergic pattern, while catheter ablation has an established role for symptomatic idiopathic RVOT VT. Unstable sustained episodes still require electrical treatment regardless of a previously reassuring idiopathic label. Document the clinical ECG before definitive treatment, and reassess if behavior changes or ventricular dysfunction appears. A benign usual course does not justify ignoring new syncope or assuming every later wide rhythm has the same mechanism. Mechanism, localization and exclusion of relevant disease are complementary assessments rather than interchangeable conclusions from one response.

Scar-mediated macroreentrant VT established by the broad QRS: Scar reentry is important when structural disease is present. QRS width alone does not establish scar, and this selected reassuring evaluation and adenosine-sensitive outflow phenotype favor triggered idiopathic VT.

Typical slow–fast AVNRT established by adenosine termination: AVNRT often terminates with adenosine, but some ventricular tachycardias do as well. The demonstrated ventricular phenotype and outflow-type morphology require interpretation rather than assigning a nodal mechanism from the drug response alone.

Left posterior fascicular reentrant VT: The common posterior fascicular phenotype has an RBBB-like pattern and superior or leftward axis and is typically verapamil sensitive. The supplied LBBB-like inferior-axis pattern and adrenergic association favor an outflow source.

ESC ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262
