questions.question: A young adult has recurrent tolerated VT with an RBBB-like QRS and superior axis. Structural evaluation is reassuring, and a previous EPS established posterior fascicular reentry. Which acute drug can specifically terminate this mechanism when pressure and conduction permit?
options: IV amiodarone
IV adenosine
IV diltiazem
IV verapamil under continuous monitoring
questions.explanation:
Verapamil-Sensitive Fascicular Ventricular Tachycardia

Correct answer: IV verapamil under continuous monitoring

Recognize the Established Purkinje-Related Mechanism

**Idiopathic posterior fascicular reentrant VT commonly produces an RBBB-like QRS with a superior axis.** The QRS can be relatively narrow compared with other VTs because specialized ventricular conduction tissue participates.

The slow, verapamil-sensitive component is part of a Purkinje-related reentry circuit. A response does not imply that the tachycardia originated in the AV node.

Anterior fascicular VT more often has an RBBB-like pattern with inferior axis, while upper septal variants can be narrower with a normal or rightward axis. These patterns guide assessment but do not replace electrophysiological confirmation when the diagnosis is uncertain.

Keep This Exception Separate From Undifferentiated WCT

**IV verapamil is appropriate for an established tolerated sensitive fascicular VT, with ECG and blood-pressure monitoring.** It is not an empirical diagnostic trial for an undifferentiated wide-complex rhythm.

Review pressure, ventricular function, conduction disease and interacting nodal drugs before administration. If unstable, prioritize electrical treatment rather than waiting to demonstrate pharmacological sensitivity.

For recurrent symptomatic idiopathic fascicular VT, ESC supports catheter ablation as a first-line definitive option after discussion of risks and alternatives. Mapping aims to interrupt the relevant circuit while limiting conduction-system injury. Do not assume that every RBBB/superior-axis VT is idiopathic: scar-related ventricular circuits and other diagnoses can overlap in appearance. Prior structural and EPS evidence in this stem makes the specific drug choice defensible. Follow symptoms and document recurrence after treatment, and reassess any new disease features. The key prescribing boundary is a confirmed mechanism with adequate hemodynamic margin, not the misconception that verapamil is safe whenever a patient with wide-complex tachycardia remains awake.

IV amiodarone: Amiodarone is a general option for selected tolerated ventricular tachycardias and may have antiarrhythmic effects here. The question asks for the specific established sensitivity of this confirmed fascicular circuit, for which verapamil is preferred.

IV adenosine: Adenosine treats AV-node-dependent SVT and can terminate selected triggered outflow VT. Reentrant posterior fascicular VT is characteristically verapamil sensitive rather than defined by adenosine sensitivity.

IV diltiazem: Diltiazem is useful for selected supraventricular rate-control problems, but membership in the nondihydropyridine calcium-channel-blocker group does not establish equivalent efficacy for fascicular reentry. Verapamil is the established mechanism-directed agent here.

questions.question: A young adult has a spontaneous ECG showing coved ST elevation of 3 mm followed by T-wave inversion in V1 recorded in the third intercostal space. Directed evaluation finds no explanatory structural disease, ischemia or electrolyte abnormality. Which interpretation is appropriate?
options: This is a type 1 Brugada pattern; a high right-precordial lead can document the finding
The finding is nondiagnostic because both V1 and V2 must show the pattern
The finding is nondiagnostic because only fourth-intercostal recordings are accepted
The finding represents a type 2 saddleback pattern
questions.explanation:
Type 1 Brugada ECG Pattern

Correct answer: This is a type 1 Brugada pattern; a high right-precordial lead can document the finding

Recognize the Morphology and Lead Position

**Type 1 Brugada ECG has coved right-precordial ST elevation of at least 2 mm, followed by T-wave inversion, in at least one of V1 or V2.** Standard fourth or high second-/third-intercostal lead positions are relevant.

Confirm calibration: 2 mm at standard gain corresponds to 0.2 mV. Do not reproduce a unit transcription error that would turn this into a 2-mV threshold.

A saddleback type 2 appearance raises a different diagnostic question. It should not be treated as a standalone type 1 result or an automatic device indication.

Separate Pattern Confirmation From Clinical Risk

**A spontaneous type 1 pattern without another explanatory heart disease supports Brugada syndrome under ESC assessment.** Exclude phenocopies such as important metabolic disturbances or ischemic and structural mimics.

An induced type 1 pattern has lower specificity and requires additional clinical context under ESC 2022, such as documented polymorphic VT/VF, arrhythmic syncope or relevant family history. Drug challenge requires an expert protocol and appropriate indication.

Fever can unmask genuine susceptibility and should not automatically be dismissed as a benign phenocopy. Treat fever promptly, review sodium-channel-blocking drugs and assess symptoms and family history. Genetic counseling and appropriate SCN5A testing can assist evaluation, but a negative result does not exclude the clinical syndrome. The ECG finding establishes a diagnostic pathway, while prior arrest, arrhythmic symptoms and spontaneous pattern guide risk assessment. An asymptomatic patient with a pattern is not automatically managed like a survivor of VF; avoid equating recognition of the tracing with a universal ICD prescription.

The finding is nondiagnostic because both V1 and V2 must show the pattern: A qualifying type 1 pattern in at least one of V1 or V2 can meet the ECG criterion. Requiring both leads can miss a genuine finding.

The finding is nondiagnostic because only fourth-intercostal recordings are accepted: High right-precordial recordings in the second or third intercostal space can reveal the pattern. Their use is deliberate rather than an automatic reason to reject the tracing.

The finding represents a type 2 saddleback pattern: Type 1 has a coved descending ST segment followed by a negative T wave. A saddleback configuration is a different pattern and is not independently equivalent to type 1.

ESC ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS genetic testing consensus, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1002/joa3.12717

questions.question: An asymptomatic adult has stable terminal QRS notching with 1.5-mm J-point elevation in two contiguous inferior leads. There is no syncope, premature familial sudden death or documented ventricular arrhythmia, and directed assessment is reassuring. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Short-QT syndrome is established by terminal QRS notching
Early-repolarization syndrome is established by the inferior-lead distribution alone
A type 1 Brugada pattern is established because J-point elevation exceeds one millimeter
An early-repolarization ECG pattern is present; the tracing alone does not establish early-repolarization syndrome or an ICD indication
questions.explanation:
Early Repolarization Pattern Versus Arrhythmic Syndrome

Correct answer: An early-repolarization ECG pattern is present; the tracing alone does not establish early-repolarization syndrome or an ICD indication

Define the Electrical Pattern Without Overdiagnosis

**Early repolarization includes terminal QRS notching or slurring with J-point elevation in inferior or lateral leads.** ESC describes elevation of at least 1 mm in at least two adjacent inferior and/or lateral leads.

Confirm that the deflection belongs to terminal ventricular activation rather than artefact or a different abnormality. ST elevation is not required by the dedicated pattern consensus, so an elevated ST segment alone should not replace the actual J-point assessment.

The pattern occurs in many healthy people. Some morphologies and clinical contexts carry greater concern, but population associations do not independently establish a dangerous syndrome in every individual.

Require the Clinical Phenotype for Syndrome Assessment

**ESC diagnoses early-repolarization syndrome in an appropriately evaluated survivor of polymorphic VT or VF with this pattern and no other explanatory heart disease.** Such a survivor requires secondary-prevention assessment rather than reassurance based on a familiar ECG variant.

An asymptomatic person with a reassuring history has a different management balance. Do not implant an ICD or prescribe suppressive quinidine solely because an incidental pattern is present.

Short-QT disease is another separate diagnosis: verify QT measurement, rate behavior and acquired causes, then integrate symptoms, family history and genetic evidence. ESC advises considering SQTS with QTc 320–360 ms and arrhythmic syncope; this conditional framework should not be reduced to a generic short-looking ST segment. Early AF or familial VF can be relevant clues. For either syndrome, avoid interpreting a genetic variant of uncertain significance as proof. New syncope or a resuscitated event warrants renewed comprehensive assessment even if a previous incidental ECG had been reassuring. Explain the distinction between an ECG descriptor and a disease associated with documented ventricular arrhythmia so follow-up is proportionate to the actual evidence.

Finding | What is needed for interpretation

Inferolateral J-point notch/slur | Pattern assessment plus symptoms and family history

Type 1 Brugada | Coved right-precordial morphology and clinical context

Short QT | Reliable QT measurement, secondary-cause exclusion and phenotype assessment

Short-QT syndrome is established by terminal QRS notching: Short-QT syndrome concerns abbreviated repolarization assessed through QT and clinical context. Terminal QRS notching does not establish a short QT or its associated syndrome.

Early-repolarization syndrome is established by the inferior-lead distribution alone: Inferior distribution can contribute to risk assessment, but a pattern is not the same as a clinical arrhythmic syndrome. The ECG finding alone does not supply the missing ventricular event.

A type 1 Brugada pattern is established because J-point elevation exceeds one millimeter: Brugada type 1 requires a specific coved right-precordial morphology, not generic inferior J-point elevation. Lead location and morphology distinguish the patterns.

questions.question: A young person has exertional syncope, a normal resting QTc and normal cardiac imaging. Monitored exercise produces increasing ventricular ectopy followed by bidirectional and polymorphic VT. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Congenital long QT syndrome as the best fit
Idiopathic RV outflow tract VT
Brugada syndrome
questions.explanation:
Exercise-Provoked Polymorphic Arrhythmia With Normal Resting ECG

Correct answer: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia

Electrical Phenotype

**Resting ECG may be normal.**

Adrenergic stress reveals abnormal intracellular calcium handling; RYR2 is a common genetic cause, with other genes including CASQ2.

Management

**Specialist inherited-arrhythmia care**, exercise/trigger counseling and nonselective beta-blockade, often nadolol.

**Add flecainide for persistent arrhythmias** despite appropriate beta-blockade; assess left cardiac sympathetic denervation in refractory cases.

**ICD decisions are individualized**, especially after arrest or refractory events.

Shocks can provoke adrenergic escalation; an ICD does not replace medication or specialist follow-up.

Congenital long QT syndrome as the best fit: LQTS can cause exertional events and occasionally a normal resting QT, but progressive adrenergic bidirectional/polymorphic ectopy with normal structure is especially characteristic of CPVT.

Idiopathic RV outflow tract VT: RVOT VT is usually monomorphic with a consistent LBBB/inferior-axis morphology, unlike the escalating bidirectional/polymorphic pattern.

Brugada syndrome: Brugada events more often occur at rest/fever with a diagnostic right-precordial pattern; this exercise-dependent calcium-handling phenotype fits CPVT better.

ESC Ventricular Arrhythmia/Sudden Death Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

questions.question: During an ARVC evaluation, a 24-year-old has T-wave inversion in V1–V3 and no complete RBBB. Under the revised 2010 Task Force framework, which interpretation is appropriate?
options: One major depolarization criterion
One minor repolarization criterion
One major repolarization criterion
One minor depolarization criterion
questions.explanation:
ARVC ECG Criteria and Conduction Exclusions

Correct answer: One major repolarization criterion

Check Age, Leads and Bundle-Branch Context

**Right-precordial T-wave inversion must be interpreted with age and conduction pattern.** In the named 2010 framework, V1–V3 inversion or extension beyond those leads in someone older than fourteen without complete RBBB is a major repolarization finding.

When complete RBBB is present, inversion through V4 is a minor criterion in that framework. Do not apply the non-RBBB rule to expected secondary repolarization changes without checking the QRS.

Juvenile and athletic patterns, lead placement and other right-heart or inflammatory disease can complicate interpretation. A criterion is not proof of a unique etiology.

Keep Electrical Categories Distinct

**Depolarization findings concern delayed ventricular activation, whereas T-wave findings concern repolarization.** Confirm reproducibility and technical quality before calling a small post-QRS deflection an epsilon wave.

A terminal activation duration of at least ==55 ms== from the S-wave nadir to QRS end in V1, V2 or V3, without complete RBBB, is a minor delayed-activation criterion under the named framework.

Integrate the tracing with ventricular imaging, arrhythmia morphology, symptoms and the pedigree. Contemporary interpretation recognizes limitations in reproducibility of some older electrical findings and the broader spectrum of arrhythmogenic disease. Do not diagnose ARVC solely because an automated ECG report mentions right-precordial inversion, and do not exclude it because an epsilon wave is absent. New exertional syncope or sustained ventricular arrhythmia demands urgent assessment independent of whether every classification item has been collected. Risk treatment follows the patient’s actual phenotype and clinical history rather than one isolated ECG label.

One major depolarization criterion: T-wave inversion concerns repolarization. A reproducible epsilon wave was a major delayed-activation finding in the 2010 framework, but no such post-QRS signal is supplied here.

One minor repolarization criterion: Adult V1–V2 inversion without complete RBBB can be a minor finding, while the supplied extension through V3 meets the major rule. The separate complete-RBBB context uses different lead requirements.

One minor depolarization criterion: Terminal activation delay and selected signal-averaged ECG abnormalities are minor delayed-activation findings. They require their own measurements and cannot be inferred from the supplied T-wave inversion.

Revised ARVC Task Force diagnostic criteria, 2010 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehq025

ESC cardiomyopathy guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad194

questions.question: A patient with advanced CKD has confirmed nonhemolyzed potassium 7.0 mmol/L, but QRS duration and T waves are not strikingly abnormal. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A normal-looking ECG does not exclude dangerous hyperkalemia or remove the need for urgent treatment
The potassium result must be artifactual because ECG changes are absent
Treatment can wait until QRS widening appears
Only calcium is needed because it removes potassium rapidly
questions.explanation:
Hyperkalemia With a Reassuring ECG

Correct answer: A normal-looking ECG does not exclude dangerous hyperkalemia or remove the need for urgent treatment

ECG Limitations

**ECG sensitivity is limited**, and severity depends on rate of rise, acid–base state and underlying disease.

Peaked T waves, loss of P waves and QRS widening are important when present but may not progress sequentially.

Urgent Management

**Monitor, confirm the context and treat the severe biochemical abnormality.**

Use appropriate intracellular-shift measures and potassium removal, including dialysis when indicated; monitor glucose with insulin therapy.

**Calcium is membrane stabilization**, especially with toxic ECG changes or instability, rather than potassium removal.

**Recheck potassium and watch rebound** after temporary shifting treatments.

The potassium result must be artifactual because ECG changes are absent: Pseudohyperkalemia requires sampling/clinical assessment; a confirmed result cannot be dismissed solely because the ECG lacks classic changes.

Treatment can wait until QRS widening appears: ECG changes do not follow a reliable obligatory sequence; waiting for conduction failure risks sudden deterioration.

Only calcium is needed because it removes potassium rapidly: IV calcium stabilizes the myocardium when indicated but does not lower total body potassium; shifting and elimination strategies address the potassium burden.

AHA Special Circumstances of Resuscitation — https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation/

questions.question: After prolonged vomiting, a patient has flat T waves, ST depression and large U waves in V2–V4. The machine reports QTc 610 ms, but T and U are partly fused. What is the best interpretation?
options: Hypokalemic repolarization abnormality with possible QU mismeasurement
Definite congenital long QT syndrome based on the machine value
Hypercalcemia shortening the ST segment
Therapeutic digoxin effect as the complete explanation
questions.explanation:
Hypokalemia and Apparent QT Prolongation

Correct answer: Hypokalemic repolarization abnormality with possible QU mismeasurement

Measurement

**Exclude a separate U wave from QT.**

When T–U fusion obscures the endpoint, use a clearer lead and manual assessment; the machine may have measured QU.

Clinical Response

**Check potassium, magnesium and renal function**, replace deficits and review QT-prolonging drugs.

Hypomagnesemia can cause refractory potassium depletion and increase ventricular arrhythmia risk.

**Do not dismiss the tracing as merely a measurement error.**

Hypokalemia itself promotes ectopy and torsades; monitor severe abnormalities and reassess the ECG after correction.

Definite congenital long QT syndrome based on the machine value: Acquired electrolyte depletion and unclear T-wave end must be addressed before diagnosing an inherited syndrome from an automated number.

Hypercalcemia shortening the ST segment: Hypercalcemia generally shortens QT through ST shortening; flat T waves and prominent U waves after vomiting favor potassium depletion.

Therapeutic digoxin effect as the complete explanation: Digoxin may cause scooped ST depression and shorter QT, but the supplied GI-loss context and prominent U waves require electrolyte assessment.

AHA ECG Monitoring Practice Standards, 2017 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000527

questions.question: A patient has a markedly abbreviated ST segment and short QT, with otherwise relatively preserved T-wave morphology. Which biochemical abnormality most directly explains this pattern?
options: Hypocalcemia
Hypercalcemia
Hypokalemia
Hypomagnesemia
questions.explanation:
Calcium and the ST Segment

Correct answer: Hypercalcemia

Repolarization Mechanism

**High calcium shortens the ventricular plateau**, abbreviating ST and QT.

Low calcium prolongs ST; the effect need not require a major change in T-wave duration.

Confirm and Distinguish

**Measure calcium and assess the clinical cause.**

Albumin and ionized calcium may matter; ECG cannot quantify the biochemical level.

**Short QT also occurs with digoxin or rare inherited disease.**

Exclude acquired causes before diagnosing short QT syndrome; severe hypercalcemia can also cause PR/QRS changes or bradyarrhythmia.

Hypocalcemia: Low calcium prolongs the plateau/ST segment and QT, producing the opposite direction of change.

Hypokalemia: Potassium depletion typically produces flat T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves rather than isolated ST shortening.

Hypomagnesemia: Magnesium depletion promotes arrhythmias and often accompanies QT-related risk; a very short ST segment points more directly to increased calcium.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

questions.question: After amitriptyline ingestion, a patient develops hypotension, QRS 148 ms and a prominent terminal R wave in aVR. Which treatment most directly targets the conduction toxicity?
options: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Intravenous magnesium as the sole targeted therapy
Intravenous amiodarone as the initial targeted treatment
Intravenous calcium gluconate as the principal antidote
questions.explanation:
Sodium-Channel Blocker Cardiotoxicity

Correct answer: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate

Toxic ECG Pattern

**Fast sodium-channel blockade slows phase-0 conduction**, widening QRS and shifting terminal forces toward aVR.

Seizures, acidosis and shock can worsen toxicity; do not wait for a drug level.

Resuscitation

**IV sodium bicarbonate boluses are titrated to improved QRS width and perfusion.**

Common initial dosing is 1–2 mEq/kg; monitor sodium, potassium and blood gas to avoid excessive alkalemia/hypernatremia.

**Support ventilation and circulation and treat seizures**, with poison-center/critical-care involvement.

**Continuous ECG reassessment is essential.**

A transient response does not establish toxin clearance; ongoing therapy depends on recurrent conduction toxicity and hemodynamics.

Intravenous magnesium as the sole targeted therapy: Magnesium is central in torsades with delayed repolarization; this pattern instead identifies sodium-channel conduction blockade requiring sodium/alkalinization therapy.

Intravenous amiodarone as the initial targeted treatment: Amiodarone is used for selected arrhythmias, but it does not reverse the toxic sodium-channel mechanism and can add hypotension or electrophysiological effects.

Intravenous calcium gluconate as the principal antidote: Calcium is used for hyperkalemic membrane stabilization or selected calcium-channel blocker poisoning; it is not the principal treatment for TCA conduction toxicity.

AHA Special Circumstances of Resuscitation: Poisoning — https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation/

questions.question: A stable patient taking digoxin has unchanged scooped lateral ST depression, mildly prolonged PR and a shortened QT. There are no new symptoms, ectopy or conduction block. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Therapeutic digoxin-related repolarization and AV nodal effects
Definite digoxin toxicity requiring antibody fragments
Acute subendocardial ischemia established by ST shape alone
Hypokalemia as the necessary explanation
questions.explanation:
Therapeutic Digoxin Effect

Correct answer: Therapeutic digoxin-related repolarization and AV nodal effects

Drug Effect Versus Toxicity

**Digoxin effect:** scooped ST depression, QT shortening and vagally mediated PR prolongation.

This pattern can occur at therapeutic exposure and is not a serum-level assay.

When to Suspect Toxicity

**New GI/neurological symptoms, ectopy or AV block** require reassessment.

Atrial tachycardia with block and bidirectional VT are important toxic patterns.

**Check renal function, potassium, magnesium and interacting drugs.**

Interpret a serum level with sampling time and clinical context; treat life-threatening toxicity rather than the ST shape alone.

Definite digoxin toxicity requiring antibody fragments: Toxicity requires integrated clinical/rhythm evidence; the stable characteristic repolarization effect alone does not establish life-threatening poisoning.

Acute subendocardial ischemia established by ST shape alone: Ischemia can coexist, but an unchanged characteristic drug pattern without ischemic symptoms does not establish acute coronary disease.

Hypokalemia as the necessary explanation: Hypokalemia can increase digoxin toxicity and produces U waves/flat T waves; it is not required to explain this stable therapeutic drug pattern.

AHA Special Circumstances of Resuscitation — https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation/

questions.question: A patient rescued after prolonged cold exposure has a core temperature of 29°C, sinus bradycardia and a prominent positive deflection at the QRS–ST junction in several leads. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Acute territorial ST-elevation infarction
Hypothermia-associated Osborn waves
Brugada type 1 pattern
Hyperkalemia as the sole mechanism
questions.explanation:
Hypothermic J Waves

Correct answer: Hypothermia-associated Osborn waves

ECG Effects

**Hypothermia can produce J waves, bradycardia and prolonged intervals.**

J-wave size often increases as temperature falls; shivering artifact may obscure the tracing.

Clinical Care

**Use controlled rewarming and continuous monitoring**, with gentle handling and correction of associated metabolic abnormalities.

**J waves are not absolutely specific to hypothermia.**

Interpret temperature, lead distribution and symptoms; reassess persistent abnormalities after rewarming.

**Severe hypothermia increases ventricular arrhythmia risk**, so the tracing should trigger appropriate resuscitation planning rather than isolated ECG labeling.

Acute territorial ST-elevation infarction: Acute occlusion remains a clinical differential, but diffuse J-point deflections with severe hypothermia and bradycardia fit temperature-related changes better than a single coronary territory.

Brugada type 1 pattern: Brugada requires characteristic coved right-precordial ST elevation with T inversion in the relevant context; generalized hypothermic J waves are not equivalent.

Hyperkalemia as the sole mechanism: Hyperkalemia commonly alters T waves, P waves and QRS conduction; the temperature-dependent QRS–ST notch is a characteristic hypothermic clue.

AHA Special Circumstances of Resuscitation — https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation/

questions.question: A pacemaker-dependent patient becomes presyncopal. Ventricular pacing spikes occur regularly, but several are not followed by QRS complexes. What is the immediate device abnormality?
options: Ventricular oversensing
Failure of ventricular capture
Ventricular undersensing
Normal fusion beats
questions.explanation:
Pacemaker Failure to Capture

Correct answer: Failure of ventricular capture

Recognize Noncapture

**Output is present but myocardial activation is absent.**

Causes include lead displacement/failure, rising threshold, metabolic disturbance and inadequate programmed output.

Urgent Response

**Assess perfusion and provide backup pacing/resuscitation if unstable.**

A pacemaker-dependent patient can deteriorate rapidly; do not wait for routine clinic follow-up.

**Arrange urgent interrogation**, check leads and reversible causes such as hyperkalemia/acidosis.

Output adjustment may restore capture, but correcting lead or metabolic pathology is essential; verify mechanical as well as electrical response.

Ventricular oversensing: Oversensing generally inhibits expected output, causing absent spikes; here stimuli are visible but fail to depolarize the ventricle.

Ventricular undersensing: Undersensing causes inappropriate pacing despite intrinsic beats; it does not primarily describe a delivered stimulus lacking the expected QRS.

Normal fusion beats: Fusion combines intrinsic and paced activation into a QRS; a spike with no ventricular depolarization is not a fusion complex.

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: A patient with a ventricular demand pacemaker develops pauses during arm movement. Interrogation shows rapid nonphysiological sensed signals and suppression of ventricular output during the pauses. What mechanism best fits?
options: Undersensing of intrinsic QRS complexes
Failure of myocardial capture
Oversensing of lead-related noise
Normal rate-responsive pacing
questions.explanation:
Pacemaker Oversensing

Correct answer: Oversensing of lead-related noise

Mechanism

**Inappropriate sensing resets/inhibits demand pacing.**

Lead fracture, insulation problems, myopotentials or electromagnetic interference can produce noise; movement association helps localize the cause.

Management

**Assess dependence and instability**, provide backup support and obtain urgent device interrogation.

**Review stored electrograms, impedance and lead integrity.**

Intermittent faults can escape a single normal measurement.

**Magnet responses differ by device and programming.**

Do not assume that a magnet universally creates safe asynchronous pacing, especially in ICDs; use a device-specific supervised plan.

Undersensing of intrinsic QRS complexes: Undersensing typically permits unnecessary pacing because intrinsic activity is missed; the device is instead detecting excessive inappropriate signals.

Failure of myocardial capture: Capture failure requires delivered pacing stimuli without depolarization; output is being inhibited before a stimulus is delivered here.

Normal rate-responsive pacing: Rate-response algorithms increase or adjust pacing with activity; they do not normally interpret lead noise as repeated intrinsic ventricular beats causing pauses.

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: In a dual-chamber pacemaker, a ventricular premature beat is followed by retrograde atrial activation. Each subsequent atrial sensed event triggers ventricular pacing after the programmed AV delay, at the upper tracking rate. What mechanism best fits?
options: Sensor-driven rate-responsive tachycardia
Endless-loop pacemaker-mediated tachycardia
Atrial flutter tracking
Ventricular tachycardia with incidental pacemaker spikes
questions.explanation:
Pacemaker-Mediated Tachycardia

Correct answer: Endless-loop pacemaker-mediated tachycardia

Circuit

**Retrograde VA conduction + atrial sensing + ventricular tracking** completes the loop.

A PVC or loss of AV synchrony can initiate it; rate is often limited by the upper tracking setting.

Terminate and Prevent

**Device interrogation confirms the sequence.**

Programming a sufficiently long postventricular atrial refractory period prevents tracking of the retrograde P wave; PMT termination algorithms can help.

**Distinguish true atrial tachyarrhythmia and sensor-driven pacing** before reprogramming.

Review VA timing and preserve appropriate exercise tracking; do not treat every paced tachycardia as intrinsic VT.

Sensor-driven rate-responsive tachycardia: Sensor-driven acceleration follows the activity/physiological sensor rather than a stable retrograde atrial–ventricular tracking loop initiated by a PVC.

Atrial flutter tracking: Flutter tracking originates from an independent rapid atrial rhythm; here each atrial signal follows ventricular activation retrogradely.

Ventricular tachycardia with incidental pacemaker spikes: The device is triggering each ventricular event after sensed atrial activity, supporting a device-mediated loop rather than an independent ventricular focus.

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: During venepuncture, a patient becomes nauseated and pale, collapses, has several brief irregular jerks, and is oriented within seconds after being placed supine. Which interpretation is most likely?
options: Psychogenic pseudosyncope solely because venepuncture is a trigger
Generalized tonic-clonic seizure established by any jerking
Reflex syncope with hypoperfusion-related myoclonic movements
Cataplexy
questions.explanation:
Convulsive Syncope Versus Epileptic Seizure

Correct answer: Reflex syncope with hypoperfusion-related myoclonic movements

Discriminating History

**Trigger, autonomic prodrome and rapid reorientation** support reflex syncope.

Brief arrhythmic jerks and urinary incontinence can occur in either syncope or seizure.

Avoid a Duration Myth

**Generalized tonic-clonic seizures often last about 1–2 minutes**, followed by postictal impairment; they do not usually require >5 minutes to qualify.

Lateral tongue bite, stereotyped aura and prolonged confusion favor seizure, but no isolated sign replaces the full account.

**Obtain witness history, examination, orthostatic vitals and ECG.**

Target EEG or neurological investigations to a credible seizure suspicion rather than reflexively ordering them for all fainting.

Psychogenic pseudosyncope solely because venepuncture is a trigger: Emotional/procedural triggers can cause genuine reflex hypotension; a functional diagnosis needs positive features and appropriate physiological correlation.

Generalized tonic-clonic seizure established by any jerking: Brief myoclonus can occur during cerebral hypoperfusion; movements alone do not establish epilepsy when the trigger, pallor and rapid recovery favor syncope.

Cataplexy: Cataplexy causes emotion-triggered loss of tone with preserved awareness; this event includes true transient loss of consciousness and presyncopal autonomic symptoms.

Correct answer: C — Reflex syncope with hypoperfusion-related myoclonic movements

Discriminating History

  • Trigger, autonomic prodrome and rapid reorientation support reflex syncope.
    • Brief arrhythmic jerks and urinary incontinence can occur in either syncope or seizure.

  • Generalized tonic-clonic seizures often last about 1–2 minutes, followed by postictal impairment; they do not usually require >5 minutes to qualify.
    • Lateral tongue bite, stereotyped aura and prolonged confusion favor seizure, but no isolated sign replaces the full account.
  • Obtain witness history, examination, orthostatic vitals and ECG.
    • Target EEG or neurological investigations to a credible seizure suspicion rather than reflexively ordering them for all fainting.

questions.question: After five minutes supine, BP is 142/82 mmHg. At one and three minutes of standing it is 116/72 and 114/70, with reproduced lightheadedness. Which diagnosis is supported?
options: Classical orthostatic hypotension
Initial orthostatic hypotension
Delayed orthostatic hypotension
POTS
questions.explanation:
Classical Orthostatic Hypotension

Correct answer: Classical orthostatic hypotension

Threshold and Timing

**Sustained SBP fall ≥20 or DBP fall ==≥10 mmHg== within 3 minutes** meets the classical threshold.

The wording is within three minutes, not only a measurement after three minutes; ESC also recognizes sustained SBP ==<90 mmHg==.

Determine the Cause

**Review volume, drugs and autonomic symptoms.**

Blunted HR compensation can suggest neurogenic disease, but beta-blockers, pacing and conduction disease confound it.

**Treat reversible contributors first**, then consider fluid/salt measures and compression when safe.

Supine hypertension, heart failure and renal disease limit indiscriminate volume expansion.

Initial orthostatic hypotension: Initial OH is a transient marked fall within roughly 15 seconds of standing; a sustained fall at one and three minutes fits classical OH.

Delayed orthostatic hypotension: Delayed OH begins beyond three minutes; the clinically significant fall is already present within the first minute.

POTS: POTS requires orthostatic tachycardia without a sustained OH-range pressure fall; this patient has a clear sustained hypotensive response.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

ESC Practical Instructions for Syncope, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy071

questions.question: A 24-year-old has six months of upright palpitations and lightheadedness relieved by lying down. HR rises from 70 to 108/min on repeated standing measurements within ten minutes; BP remains stable. Anemia, dehydration, thyroid disease and medication effects are excluded. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Classical orthostatic hypotension
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome
Inappropriate sinus tachycardia
Paroxysmal AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome

Correct answer: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

Required Features

**Sustained HR rise ≥30/min in adults** within ten minutes; ≥40/min for ages 12–19.

Require chronic orthostatic symptoms, generally ≥3 months, no sustained OH-range BP fall and no better explanation.

Assessment and Care

**Repeat standardized supine-to-standing HR/BP measurements.**

A single transient peak is insufficient; consider morning variability and confounders.

**Begin individualized fluid/salt, compression and graded exercise measures** when appropriate.

Medication selection depends on HR, pressure and symptoms; POTS is not diagnosed solely from a wearable pulse alert or from unexplained fatigue.

Classical orthostatic hypotension: Classical OH requires a sustained pressure fall; stable BP with a sustained symptomatic tachycardic response supports a different orthostatic syndrome.

Inappropriate sinus tachycardia: IST more often includes excessive resting/average heart rate and symptoms beyond posture; a normal supine HR with a reproducible upright response favors POTS.

Paroxysmal AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: AVNRT typically starts and stops abruptly as a reentrant rhythm; the sustained posture-linked sinus acceleration described here is not that pattern.

Canadian Cardiovascular Society Position Statement on POTS, 2020 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cjca.2019.12.024

questions.question: A patient has recurrent unexplained syncope every three to four months. Initial assessment and echo are unrevealing, and there is no indication for immediate ICD/pacing or inpatient high-risk treatment. Which strategy best seeks symptom–rhythm correlation?
options: A single 24-hour Holter recording
Implantable loop recorder
A 48-hour inpatient telemetry admission as the definitive long-term test
Routine invasive EPS in every such patient
questions.explanation:
Monitoring Infrequent Unexplained Syncope

Correct answer: Implantable loop recorder

Match Monitoring to Event Frequency

**Long-term recording increases the chance of capturing the spontaneous event.**

The objective is a rhythm correlated with symptoms, not merely incidental ectopy.

Selection and Interpretation

**ILR is appropriate in selected recurrent unexplained syncope** when recurrence is likely and immediate high-risk therapy is not required.

**A normal short monitor does not exclude arrhythmia.**

External monitoring suits sufficiently frequent episodes; high-risk findings require prompt evaluation rather than waiting months for an ILR event.

**Continue assessment for nonarrhythmic causes** even after implantation.

A single 24-hour Holter recording: Holter is useful when symptoms are frequent; a one-day window is unlikely to capture an event recurring every few months.

A 48-hour inpatient telemetry admission as the definitive long-term test: Telemetry is appropriate for immediate high-risk assessment but a brief admission has low yield for this infrequent stable recurrence pattern.

Routine invasive EPS in every such patient: EPS is useful in selected substrates or conduction disease; it is not the highest-yield universal test in a structurally reassuring, infrequent-event presentation.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

questions.question: A patient with an uncertain history has typical symptoms reproduced on tilt, preceded by progressive hypotension and then bradycardia. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: The result demonstrates susceptibility to a reflex hypotensive response, interpreted with the spontaneous history
It excludes an arrhythmic cause for every previous event
It establishes a pacemaker indication from hypotension alone
It establishes epilepsy because consciousness was lost during testing
questions.explanation:
Interpreting a Positive Tilt Test

Correct answer: The result demonstrates susceptibility to a reflex hypotensive response, interpreted with the spontaneous history

Physiological Meaning

**Tilt reproduces symptoms with monitored HR and BP.**

The timing of hypotension versus bradycardia helps characterize vasodepressor, cardioinhibitory or mixed responses.

Limits

**A positive result is contextual evidence**, not a universal explanation of every attack.

A negative result does not exclude reflex syncope either.

**Tilt can also evaluate delayed OH or apparent functional events** using appropriate physiological recording.

**Use the spontaneous history and risk profile** to decide whether additional rhythm or structural assessment is still needed.

It excludes an arrhythmic cause for every previous event: Reflex susceptibility can coexist with cardiac disease; a positive tilt does not prove that all spontaneous episodes share the same mechanism.

It establishes a pacemaker indication from hypotension alone: Pacing targets selected cardioinhibitory mechanisms and cannot directly reverse vasodilation; tilt-induced hypotension alone is not sufficient.

It establishes epilepsy because consciousness was lost during testing: Loss of consciousness with documented hypotension/bradycardia supports hypoperfusion; epileptic diagnosis requires different supporting evidence.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

ESC Practical Instructions for Syncope, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy071

questions.question: During appropriately monitored carotid sinus massage in a 72-year-old with unexplained falls, a 4-second pause occurs but no spontaneous-type symptom is reproduced. What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity; carotid sinus syndrome is not established by the pause alone
Definite carotid sinus syndrome requiring pacing regardless of symptom correlation
A normal response because asystole is less than six seconds
Proof of intrinsic sinus node disease
questions.explanation:
Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity Versus Syndrome

Correct answer: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity; carotid sinus syndrome is not established by the pause alone

Diagnostic Distinction

**Hypersensitivity:** ventricular pause >3 seconds and/or SBP fall ==>50 mmHg== during massage.

Carotid sinus syndrome requires compatible spontaneous events reproduced by the test; symptom-producing pauses are often longer.

Safe Testing

**Use ECG and beat-to-beat BP monitoring** in an appropriate clinical setting, usually age >40 with a compatible unexplained reflex presentation.

**Assess cerebrovascular/carotid contraindications first.**

Recent stroke/TIA or significant carotid stenosis requires avoidance or specialist risk assessment; the test is not an unmonitored bedside experiment.

Definite carotid sinus syndrome requiring pacing regardless of symptom correlation: Asymptomatic hypersensitivity is common in older people; syndrome diagnosis requires reproduction of compatible spontaneous symptoms and clinical correlation.

A normal response because asystole is less than six seconds: A pause exceeding three seconds meets the conventional hypersensitivity criterion; absence of symptoms limits the syndrome inference rather than making the response normal.

Proof of intrinsic sinus node disease: A provoked reflex pause does not by itself establish intrinsic sinus-node failure; mechanism and spontaneous rhythm evidence must be distinguished.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

ESC Practical Instructions for Syncope, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy071

questions.question: A patient with recurrent vasovagal episodes consistently has 30–60 seconds of warmth, nausea and visual dimming before collapse. Which preventive action is most appropriate at the onset of this prodrome?
options: Remain upright and walk briskly to restore blood pressure
Sit or lie safely, with leg/abdominal muscle tensing or handgrip while still able
Take an extra beta-blocker dose immediately
Use breath-holding with prolonged straining as the main maneuver
questions.explanation:
Counterpressure Maneuvers in Reflex Syncope

Correct answer: Sit or lie safely, with leg/abdominal muscle tensing or handgrip while still able

Mechanism

**Muscle contraction increases venous return and vascular resistance.**

Leg crossing with tensing, buttock/abdominal contraction and handgrip can delay or abort a prodromal episode.

Selection and Safety

**A recognizable prodrome is essential.**

Sudden unwarned events may not allow a maneuver and need further risk assessment.

**Lie down before attempting to walk elsewhere.**

Avoid injury; use hydration, trigger avoidance and salt measures only when compatible with BP, cardiac and renal status.

**Persistent injurious recurrence warrants reassessment**, rather than relying solely on self-rescue maneuvers.

Remain upright and walk briskly to restore blood pressure: Walking during evolving presyncope risks a fall; reducing orthostatic stress and using safe counterpressure are more appropriate.

Take an extra beta-blocker dose immediately: Beta-blockade does not provide rapid rescue from reflex hypotension and may blunt compensatory responses; it is not the appropriate prodromal action.

Use breath-holding with prolonged straining as the main maneuver: A sustained Valsalva strain can reduce venous return; it differs from evidence-based muscle counterpressure with safe posture.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

questions.question: A young adult with a low-BP phenotype continues frequent vasovagal syncope despite education, hydration and counterpressure training. There is no hypertension or urinary retention. Which drug reduced recurrence in POST-4 and is a reasonable option?
options: Paroxetine
Metoprolol
Midodrine
Fludrocortisone
questions.explanation:
Midodrine for Recurrent Vasovagal Syncope

Correct answer: Midodrine

Evidence and Action

**Midodrine is an alpha-1 agonist** that supports vascular tone.

POST-4 found recurrence in ==42%== with midodrine versus ==61%== with placebo in a selected predominantly young population; benefit is not universal.

Practical Use

**Typically ==2.5–10 mg== three times daily during waking hours**, titrated to symptoms and pressure.

Avoid dosing near bedtime, commonly within four hours; monitor supine BP.

**Watch urinary retention, scalp tingling and piloerection.**

Evidence in selected low-risk patients should not replace investigation of possible cardiac syncope or treatment of orthostatic drug/volume causes.

Paroxetine: SSRIs have been studied in selected refractory patients, but evidence is limited and heterogeneous; paroxetine was not the POST-4 intervention.

Metoprolol: Beta-blockers have not shown reliable benefit for typical young vasovagal patients; metoprolol was not the intervention tested in POST-4.

Fludrocortisone: Volume expansion can help selected low-BP patients, but fludrocortisone was evaluated in POST-2; it was not the drug producing the stated POST-4 result.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

questions.question: A patient with orthostatic symptoms starts fludrocortisone and subsequently develops ankle edema, higher supine BP and potassium 3.1 mmol/L. Which mechanism best explains the adverse-effect cluster?
options: Mineralocorticoid-mediated sodium retention and renal potassium loss
Direct alpha-1 vasoconstriction without volume expansion
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition at autonomic ganglia
Norepinephrine precursor conversion
questions.explanation:
Fludrocortisone Safety in Orthostatic Hypotension

Correct answer: Mineralocorticoid-mediated sodium retention and renal potassium loss

Drug Mechanism

**Fludrocortisone expands extracellular volume** and can increase vascular responsiveness.

Typical low doses are ==0.05–0.1 mg== daily, cautiously up to about ==0.2 mg==/day in selected patients.

Monitoring and Response

**Review or reduce treatment and correct potassium as appropriate.**

Monitor weight, edema, supine/standing pressure and renal function.

**Heart failure, significant edema and supine hypertension limit use.**

Volume expansion is not benign; reconsider reversible causes, abdominal compression and alternative strategies rather than escalating automatically.

**Treatment aims to improve upright function**, not simply normalize every BP reading.

Direct alpha-1 vasoconstriction without volume expansion: That describes midodrine more closely; the edema and potassium loss point to mineralocorticoid action.

Acetylcholinesterase inhibition at autonomic ganglia: Pyridostigmine has cholinergic effects such as diarrhea and salivation; it does not explain this sodium-retention pattern.

Norepinephrine precursor conversion: Droxidopa can raise supine BP but is not a mineralocorticoid and does not characteristically cause this potassium-wasting cluster.

questions.question: A 66-year-old has severe recurrent unpredictable syncope with injuries despite conservative care. An ILR records an 8-second asystolic pause during a typical event; reversible causes have been excluded. Which strategy is supported?
options: Withhold pacing because all reflex syncope is purely vasodepressor
Use pacing only if the baseline resting HR is below 40/min
Evaluate for dual-chamber pacing for documented cardioinhibitory reflex syncope
Implant an ICD because any prolonged pause predicts ventricular fibrillation
questions.explanation:
Pacing Selected Reflex Syncope

Correct answer: Evaluate for dual-chamber pacing for documented cardioinhibitory reflex syncope

Selection

**Selected patients >40 with severe recurrent unpredictable events and documented asystole** may benefit from dual-chamber pacing.

Common spontaneous pause thresholds: >3 seconds with symptoms or >6 seconds without symptoms, interpreted in the full clinical setting.

Evidence and Limitations

**BioSync CLS supports selected older patients with tilt-induced asystole**, not indiscriminate pacing of young typical fainters.

**Pacing cannot directly correct vasodilation.**

A major hypotensive component may still cause recurrence; continue preventive measures and realistic counseling.

**Establish symptom–rhythm correlation** and exclude reversible bradycardia before an implant decision.

Withhold pacing because all reflex syncope is purely vasodepressor: Reflex events can have a dominant cardioinhibitory component; documented symptomatic asystole in a selected older patient changes the treatment options.

Use pacing only if the baseline resting HR is below 40/min: Intermittent symptomatic asystole can justify pacing despite a normal resting rate; a persistent bradycardia threshold is not required here.

Implant an ICD because any prolonged pause predicts ventricular fibrillation: An asystolic reflex event is not itself an ICD indication; defibrillation addresses malignant tachyarrhythmia risk, not this documented mechanism.

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

BioSync CLS randomized trial, 2021 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33279955/

questions.question: Two athletes faint: patient A loses consciousness while sprinting without warning; patient B becomes nauseated and faints after stopping abruptly in heat. Which interpretation should guide the initial evaluation?
options: Both events establish benign vasovagal syncope because the patients are athletes
During-exercise syncope in A raises greater concern for structural or arrhythmic disease
Postexercise timing in B proves a malignant ventricular arrhythmia
A normal resting ECG would exclude cardiac disease in A
questions.explanation:
Syncope During Versus After Exercise

Correct answer: During-exercise syncope in A raises greater concern for structural or arrhythmic disease

Mechanisms

**During exertion:** consider outflow obstruction, ischemia, coronary anomaly or exercise-triggered arrhythmia.

After stopping, venous pooling and ongoing vasodilation can precipitate reflex hypotension.

Investigate Safely

**History, examination and ECG are initial requirements.**

Use echo and supervised exercise/rhythm assessment according to findings; do not prescribe an unsupervised exertional challenge.

**Assess family history and previous episodes**, and restrict risky activity pending clarification when cardiac syncope is suspected.

**Timing informs probability, not certainty**; persistent high-risk features in either patient require evaluation.

Both events establish benign vasovagal syncope because the patients are athletes: Athletic status does not exclude cardiomyopathy, coronary anomalies or channelopathy; abrupt loss during exertion needs urgent risk assessment.

Postexercise timing in B proves a malignant ventricular arrhythmia: Postexercise muscle-pump withdrawal and persistent vasodilation can cause reflex/orthostatic syncope; the autonomic prodrome supports that possibility.

A normal resting ECG would exclude cardiac disease in A: CPVT and some structural/coronary disorders may have a normal resting ECG; the exertional history still warrants directed testing.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

ESC Ventricular Arrhythmia/Sudden Death Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

questions.question: During a monitored tilt/video-EEG study, a typical prolonged episode of apparent unresponsiveness occurs with closed eyes, preserved BP and HR, and normal waking EEG activity. What diagnosis is most strongly supported?
options: Generalized epileptic seizure
Vasodepressor syncope
Psychogenic pseudosyncope
Cardioinhibitory syncope
questions.explanation:
Psychogenic Pseudosyncope

Correct answer: Psychogenic pseudosyncope

Positive Diagnosis

**A typical attack recorded without hemodynamic or EEG evidence of cerebral hypoperfusion** provides positive diagnostic evidence.

Closed eyes and long duration are clues, not standalone proof; verify the episode resembles spontaneous events.

Explain and Treat

**Describe the condition respectfully as involuntary and real.**

Avoid suggesting fabrication; offer a clear explanation and appropriate psychological/functional-disorder care.

**Consider coexisting true syncope or epilepsy** when other event types differ.

**Do not diagnose by normal interepisode tests alone** or simply by the presence of anxiety.

Generalized epileptic seizure: The recorded typical episode lacks an ictal pattern and shows preserved waking activity; the evidence favors a functional event rather than generalized epileptic loss of consciousness.

Vasodepressor syncope: Genuine vasodepressor syncope requires a fall in perfusion pressure; stable measured hemodynamics and preserved waking EEG during the typical event argue against it.

Cardioinhibitory syncope: A cardioinhibitory event would show clinically relevant bradycardia/asystole with hypoperfusion, absent during this recorded episode.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

ESC Practical Instructions for Syncope, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy071
